You don't have to use an agent (broker, as you call it), but it is strongly advised. In some counties lawyers are required, in some not. Check your local requirements. Sovereign immunity is the state's ultimate "get out of bankruptcy free" card.  After all, the state has a hand in defining what bankruptcy even is in their state.  Federal law is a framework, states customize it from there.   The state's simplest tactic is to simply not pay you.  And leave you scrambling to the courthouse for redress. Is that an automatic win?  Not really, the State can plead sovereign immunity, e.g. Hans v. Louisiana, Alden v. Maine.     You could try to pierce that sovereign immunity, essentially you'd be in Federal court trying to force the state into bankruptcy.  This would pit State authority against Federal authority.  The Feds are just as likely to come in on the state's side, and you lose.  Best scenario, it's a knock-down drag-out all the way to the Supreme Court.  You would have to be one heck of a creditor for the legal fees to be worth your trouble.  States don't make a habit of this because if they did, no one would lend money to them, and this would be rather bad for the economy all around.  So business and government work really hard to avert it.  But it always stands as their "nuclear option".  And you gotta know that when loaning money to States.

There is no cure for psoriasis, but it can be managed with treatment. The goals of treatment are to slow the growth of skin cells, reduce inflammation, and alleviate symptoms such as itching, redness, and scaling. Treatment options for psoriasis include topical medications, light therapy, and oral or injectable medications. The specific treatment plan will depend on the type and severity of the psoriasis, as well as the individual's preference and overall health.

Topical medications, which are applied to the skin, include corticosteroids, vitamin D analogues, and topical retinoids. These medications can help to reduce inflammation and slow the growth of skin cells. Light therapy, also known as phototherapy, involves exposing the skin to controlled amounts of natural or artificial light. This can help to reduce inflammation and slow the growth of skin cells.

Oral or injectable medications, also known as systemic therapies, are taken by mouth or injected into the body. These include medications such as methotrexate, cyclosporine, and biologics. Biologics are a newer type of medication that targets specific parts of the immune system. These medications can be effective, but they can also have serious side effects, so they are usually reserved for more severe cases of psoriasis or when other treatments have not been successful.

It is important to work closely with a dermatologist or other healthcare provider to determine the best treatment plan for you or your loved one. It may take some time to find the right combination of treatments that effectively manage the psoriasis, but with proper treatment, it is possible to reduce the severity of symptoms and improve quality of life.

Eat moderate amounts of healthy fats: Healthy fats such as monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fats can help lower triglycerides. These can be found in foods like olive oil, nuts, and fatty fish like salmon.

Limit alcohol: Alcohol can raise triglycerides, so it's important to limit your intake or avoid it altogether.

It's also important to speak with your healthcare provider about your diet and any recommended changes. They can provide personalized guidance based on your specific needs and medical history.

Researchers may have deciphered the oldest known scrap of alphabetic writing yet discovered, and it may be a nearly 4,500-year-old gift tag. 

A clay cylinder found in a tomb holding six skeletons in northern Syria bears the word “silanu,” which may be a name, says Glenn Schwartz, an archaeologist at Johns Hopkins University. Schwartz discovered the finger-sized cylinder, along with three others bearing similar etchings, in a tomb at Tell Umm el-Marra, an ancient city that sits between modern-day Aleppo and the Euphrates River. 

Alphabets break words into single vowels and consonants and typically require only 20 to 40 characters. That makes alphabetic systems more streamlined and easier to learn than the writing systems that came before—Egyptian hieroglyphs and Mesopotamian cuneiform. Those systems used hundreds of symbols that mainly represented words and syllables rather than individual sounds. Scientists previously thought that the first alphabet was created around 1900 B.C.E. by people speaking a Semitic language on the Sinai Peninsula in what is now Egypt. That alphabet, called Proto-Sinaitic, is based on hieroglyphic symbols repurposed as letters. The new finding suggests instead that people in farther-flung reaches of the Near East experimented with hieroglyph-derived letters much earlier. 

“It changes the entire narrative of how the alphabet was introduced,” Schwartz says. Small holes drilled into the cylinders could have been used to string them on thread. As such, the clay structures could have served as labels for goods; Silanu might have been either the recipient or sender of some of the jars of food and beverage placed in the tomb to accompany its occupants into the afterlife, Schwartz says.* The tomb likely belonged to a wealthy and powerful family in the city. 

Archaeologists first found the cylinders in 2004, and radiocarbon analysis indicated the clay dated back to about 2400 B.C.E. In 2021 Schwartz described the cylinders in an Italian journal called Pasiphae. The research didn’t get much attention, in part because Schwartz was cautious in pushing his interpretation of the inscriptions as alphabetic letters. “I probably was too timid,” he says. 

He presented a more confident interpretation this week at the annual meeting of the American Society of Overseas Research, held in Boston. Some researchers, who had access to only a few snapshots of the cylinders prior to the talk, said they were looking forward to more evidence that the inscriptions represent an alphabet rather than another type of writing system. “When you only have a few very short inscriptions, it can be difficult to tell how many signs the system has,” says Philippa Steele, a senior researcher in classics at the University of Cambridge. With so few signs to work from, she says, it’s hard to be sure that the new etchings really match up with known Proto-Sinaitic writing rather than resemble it by coincidence. “I think we have to hope for more finds,” she says. 

Others are convinced. “It’s an alphabet,” says Silvia Ferrara, a professor in early languages at the University of Bologna in Italy, who was not involved in the work. “It’s easy-peasy. I’m used to much tougher things.” 

“The morphology of the letters on the cylinder seals parallels quite nicely that of the existing corpus of early alphabetic writing,” adds Christopher Rollston, a professor of biblical and Near Eastern languages and civilizations at George Washington University, who was not involved in the new research but did study under Schwartz as a graduate student. 

While the developers of the first alphabet were once thought to be living within Egyptian society, Egyptians and Syrians had extensive trade networks, Ferrara says, and many populations around the Middle East were likely familiar with the Egyptian writing system. 

“It’s not that surprising,” she says, “knowing how far and wide these things traveled.”

Last year, Emily Anadu answered a call from New York City’s Parks and Recreation Department. “Emily, I’m mad at you,” the man on the other end of the line told her. Anadu, 45, and thousands of other Brooklynites had just convened in Fort Greene Park for the Lay Out, an annual gathering the Sunday before Juneteenth. People come together to eat, buy clothes and crafts, and just bond with one another. “Oh, no,” Anadu replied, “did we do something wrong?” “No,” he said. “You didn’t leave anything for us to do.” Attendees and organizers had returned the park in better condition than it was given. That spirit of help and community is nothing new for residents of this Brooklyn enclave, despite changes to the neighborhood over the past few decades, but it is something they’re working to protect and prioritize. A storied history Decades ago, Fort Greene, a section of Brooklyn just off the Manhattan Bridge, was largely populated by first-time-homeowning Black families living on tree-lined streets where the sky’s view inspired limitless possibilities. It was a place where folks knew their butcher’s name. Kids played outside till dusk. You saw the same people every day. The neighborhood became a mecca for art and culture, championed by filmmaker and hometown hero Spike Lee, who set his first movies there. In the 1840s, Walt Whitman helped found Fort Greene Park, the neighborhood’s beating heart, and almost a century later, Richard Wright wrote parts of Native Son in the 30-acre green space. “It was more family oriented, and you felt that family love. Every parent had permission to check someone’s child,” says Carlos Jones, 56, CEO and co-founder of Switching Lifestylez, a group of volunteers in Fort Greene who help de-¬escalate conflict among youth. On any given day, members might walk kids home from school, step in if they see trouble brewing or just lend an ear. “Now, it’s totally different, but we are bringing that vibe back,” he says of this 2024 Reader’s Digest Nicest Places in America finalist. A community worth protecting Things have changed, as anyone would expect. Skyrocketing housing costs and stark economic disparity between longtime residents and newer, wealthier residents have forced lifelong Fort Greeners out of certain parts of the neighborhood, if not out entirely. Amid it all, one thing remains firm: an intrinsic sense of both camaraderie and mutual support. It’s that sense of belonging that the Lay Out aims to protect. The idea was born in a group chat during 2020’s Black Lives Matter marches—Anadu and friends just wanted to create a safe space in the park, which is beloved to Fort Greeners. Anadu knows it so well, she can follow its pathways while reading a book. During the COVID-19 lockdowns, she picked up trash alongside maintenance crews on her daily walks. “I’m desperately trying to hold on to the history of this neighborhood, trying to make sure that Black people always have a presence,” says Anadu. The Lay Out is more than a celebration in the park. Its organizers have created an entire ecosystem, with a network of more than 500 Black-owned businesses and cooking classes whose ticket proceeds keep community fridges stocked with delicious food, free for the taking, to name a few ongoing efforts. But Anadu stresses how important simply gathering in Fort Greene Park, a space that felt increasingly encroached upon, can be for residents to bask in the joy of shared connection. “It was about reclaiming space, reclaiming each other, and this idea that peace is a form of resistance,” she says. The neighborhood is a master class in preserving the mores of old while making just enough room for what’s new, dynamic and curative. “I want people to see we aren’t like every other community,” says Jones. “Fort Greene is a wonderful place with a vibe like no other.”

Regarding the opportunity cost comparison, consider the following two scenarios assuming a three-year lease: Option A: Keep your current car for three years In this scenario, you start with a car that's worth $10,000 and end with a car that's worth $7,000 after three years. Option B: Sell your current car, invest proceeds, lease new car Here, you'll start out with $10,000 and invest it.  You'll start with $10,000 in cash from the sale of your old car, and end with $10,000 plus investment gains. You'll have to estimate the return of your investment based on your investing style.   Option C: Use the $10k from proceeds as down payment for new car In this scenario you'll get a reduction in finance charges on your lease, but you'll be out $10,000 at the end. Overall Cost Comparison To compare the total cost to own your current car versus replacing it with a new leased car, first look up the cost of ownership for your current car for the same term as the lease you're considering.  Edmunds offers this research and calls it True Cost to Own.   Specifically, you'll want to include depreciation, fuel, insurance, maintenance and repairs.  If you still owe money you should also factor the remaining payments.  So the formula is: Cost to keep car = Depreciation + Fuel + Insurance + Maintenance + Repairs On the lease side consider taxes and fees, all lease payments, fuel, and maintenance.  Assume repairs will be covered under warranty.  Assume you will put down no money on the lease and you will finance fees, taxes, title, and license when calculating lease payments.  You also need to consider the cost to pay off your current car's loan if applicable.  Then you should subtract the gains you expect from investing for three years the proceeds from the sale of your car. Assume that repairs will be covered under warranty.  The formula to lease looks like: Lease Cost = Fuel + Insurance + Maintenance + Lease payments - (gains from investing $10k) For option C, where you use the $10k from proceeds as down payment for new lease, it will be: Lease Cost = Fuel + Insurance + Maintenance + Lease payments + $10,000 A somewhat intangible factor to consider is that you'll have to pay for body damage to a leased car at the end of the lease, whereas you are obviously free to leave damage unrepaired on your own vehicle.

Nonalcoholic beverages used to be the butt of jokes. Now, they’re the fastest-growing sector of the alcohol market. Sales of nonalcoholic beer, wine and liquor increased by 32 percent from 2022 to 2023, while total alcohol sales grew by just 1 percent. As of early 2024, the top-selling beer at Whole Foods was nonalcoholic. This growth likely stems from increasing awareness of the health harms of alcohol and a rising interest in sobriety and moderation. One recent study found that health consciousness, curiosity and a desire to avoid the negative effects of alcohol (like hangovers) were among people’s top reasons for consuming nonalcoholic beverages. There are also many more — and better — nonalcoholic options on the market today. So, how much healthier are nonalcoholic (or “NA”) beverages than the real deal? Are they safe for everyone? And do they contain other ingredients people should watch out for? What is a ‘nonalcoholic beverage’? To qualify as nonalcoholic, a beverage must have less than 0.5 percent alcohol by volume (A.B.V.). Traditionally, brands use methods like filtration or distillation to remove the alcohol from their products. Newer techniques alter the fermentation process, so the sugar in the beverage isn’t turned into alcohol. Other drinks marketed as alcohol alternatives don’t try to mimic beer, wine or liquor and are made with juice or botanicals. The main harmful ingredient in alcoholic beverages — the one that damages the liver and contributes to cancer — is the alcohol, so once that’s been almost entirely removed, the health risks associated with booze pretty much disappear. “From a health perspective, very small amounts of alcohol in your drink probably don’t make a huge deal of difference,” said John Holmes, a professor of alcohol policy at the University of Sheffield in England. It’s possible you could consume a substantial amount of alcohol by drinking NA beverages, “but it would be a lot of work,” said Dr. Tim Naimi, the director of the University of Victoria’s Canadian Institute for Substance Use Research. “You’d have to drink 20 cans of 0.5 percent A.B.V. beer to get even up to two drinks a day.” However, the experts cautioned that a drink with less than 0.5 percent alcohol could still cause problems in some cases. For people with an alcohol use disorder, substituting nonalcoholic beer, wine or liquor could help them cut down on their drinking or stop completely, said Molly Bowdring, a postdoctoral scholar in clinical psychology at Stanford University. But these beverages could also serve as a trigger for relapse. “They’re so similar in taste and flavor,” she said. “That can make it a helpful substitute, but it also includes all of those cues that might activate craving.” For pregnant women, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists hasn’t weighed in on NA beverages specifically, but its website states: “There is no safe amount or type of alcohol use during pregnancy.” For people with other conditions that can be negatively affected by alcohol, like liver disease, the experts recommended asking a doctor if nonalcoholic beverages were OK to drink. Alcohol alternatives made with juice or botanicals don’t come with the concerns around alcoholic content, but they can have other problematic ingredients, so it’s important to read labels closely. For example, some drinks contain CBD or THC, or plants like ashwagandha, which has been linked to liver injury and could be harmful during pregnancy. Can they improve your health? Data suggest that over 80 percent of people who purchase nonalcoholic beverages also buy alcoholic ones. And as of 2022, NA products made up less than 1 percent of total alcohol sales. A young saber-toothed cat, no bigger than a medium-sized house pet, has emerged from Siberia’s permafrost so intact that its stubby whiskers, downy fur, and even the folds around its paw pads remain visible. Local reindeer herders discovered the frozen cub last August along a riverbank in Yakutia, a region already famous for yielding the remains of woolly mammoths and extinct bison. But this is the first time researchers have seen a saber-toothed cat preserved with such incredible detail. The cub’s species, likely a type of Homotherium—an extinct genus known from scattered fossils—roamed Eurasia over 20,000 years ago, stalking steppe bison and horses under unforgiving Ice Age skies.

Unlike typical fossilized bones pried from rock layers, this cub is a natural freeze-dried mummy: its skin, muscles, stomach contents, and even internal organs appear astonishingly intact. “We’ve had fragments and partial skeletons of saber-toothed cats from across the Northern Hemisphere,” says Dr. Albert Protopopov, head of the mammoth fauna studies department at the Academy of Sciences in Yakutsk. “But nothing comes close to this. It’s as though we’ve met the animal only yesterday.”

**Preservation in the permafrost**  
The cub, estimated to be just a few months old at death, likely ended up entombed after tumbling into a natural trap—perhaps a small ravine or a concealed hole. Once buried, it remained in permafrost that never fully thawed, even during interglacial warm spells. The region, located along the remote Tirekhtyakh River, has previously yielded cave lion cubs and a young woolly rhino, but never a saber-toothed cat. The discovery underscores just how vast and relatively unexplored these northern deposits remain.

“When I saw the first photographs sent by the local finders, I had to catch my breath,” says Dr. Love Dalén, an evolutionary geneticist at the Centre for Palaeogenetics in Stockholm, who has collaborated on similar permafrost discoveries. “We have cave lion cubs from this region, but a Homotherium kitten is next-level rare. It’s a bridge straight into the past, unfiltered by the usual decay.”

**Hunting habits and anatomy**  
Saber-toothed cats—which included several genera, the most famous being North and South American Smilodon—were top predators that took down large herbivores. But in Eurasia, Homotherium was a different beast from its American cousins: built for endurance rather than brute strength, with somewhat shorter upper canines that curved elegantly. This mummy may confirm theories about Homotherium’s body proportions, coat patterns, and even how its baby teeth erupted compared to modern big cats.

Without traditional fur patterns or living relatives, no one is entirely certain what color these cats were. Many artists paint them as tawny or patched with stripes. Now scientists can examine the cub’s coat under the microscope and apply mass spectrometry to tease out pigments. “If we recover original melanin molecules,” says Dr. Edana Lord, a molecular biologist specializing in ancient DNA at Stockholm University, “we could say something about its coat color—dark, light, maybe even banded with subtle markings. That’s the kind of detail we rarely get from fossils.”

**Genetic insights**  
Because the cub’s soft tissues are intact, the team expects to retrieve high-quality genetic material. Genetic sequencing can yield far more than a family tree: it might hint at adaptations for hunting in low-light conditions, tolerance of frigid climates, or metabolic quirks that helped the species survive in an ecosystem dominated by mammoths, woolly rhinoceroses, and giant deer.

“For a start, we want to confirm it’s a Homotherium,” says Protopopov. “We assume that from skull morphology and tooth shape, but genetics will settle it. Then we can see how closely related it is to Homotherium populations known from central Europe or Alaska. Were there distinct lineages roaming these steppes, or did they form one large population?”

Moreover, stable isotope analysis of the cub’s tissues might reveal what its mother ate, since nursing offspring often carry chemical signatures inherited from maternal milk. By comparing these isotopes with known prey species from the region, scientists can narrow down the menu of a saber-toothed cat family. “If we find that its mother’s diet leaned heavily on young horses, that’s one clue to hunting strategy,” says Dalén. “If, on the other hand, reindeer or muskox dominated, that suggests different prey selection.”

**Beyond basic biology**  
This mummy also hints at social behaviors. Did Homotherium mothers stash their cubs in dens? Were they solitary or did they hunt cooperatively, like modern lions? The cub’s find spot—far from deep caves—suggests it might have been sheltered in some above-ground hideout, possibly under shrubs or in a small depression. One can imagine a mother cat leaving her offspring briefly while she pursued prey, only to never return. But until more individuals turn up, it’s hard to be certain.

“We’re piecing together a puzzle from just one fragment,” says Dr. Yukiko Tatsuro, a paleontologist at Hokkaido University who has worked on cave lion cubs but not involved in this study. “But even one well-preserved cub can test or refine existing assumptions. Maybe Homotherium was less cave-oriented, or maybe they used a wider range of habitats than we once thought.”

**Darker realities and cultural interest**  
While the scientific value is enormous, there’s a quiet undercurrent of loss. The cub’s species—and the entire Pleistocene megafauna—disappeared thousands of years ago, influenced by shifting climates and possibly human activity. Now, as permafrost warms due to climate change, more such remains may surface. This offers unprecedented opportunities, but it also exposes delicate finds to decay and looting. Local communities, scientists, and regional authorities must balance curiosity with conservation.

The mummy will likely reside in a specialized cold-storage facility at the Academy of Sciences in Yakutsk, where experts will X-ray its skeletal structure and carry out careful dissections of tiny tissue samples. Tourists and students might eventually see it on display once initial research concludes. Already, field rumors have sparked excitement. Social media chatter in Yakutsk’s small cafés, where paleontologists sometimes gather after long days in cold labs, bubbles with speculation: Will we be able to see the spots on its fur, read its last meal from its intestines, or even reconstruct its DNA?

**No neat final word**  
There’s no final verdict yet—just a flurry of tests and waiting for data. Scientists will be cautious. Each step is painstaking: a small snippet of ear tissue to test for pigments, a tiny bone sample for isotopes. Every result will stir debate, spark new hypotheses. The cub, silent and still after so many millennia, now speaks volumes through its preserved flesh.

Protopopov puts it plainly: “We’re suddenly face-to-face with an ancient predator that lived in a world we barely understand. I expect it will keep us busy for years, maybe decades.”

Share sales & purchases are accounted only on the balance sheet & cash flow statement although their effects are seen on the income statement. Remember, the balance sheet is like a snapshot in time of all accrued accounts; it's like looking at a glass of water and noting the level.  The cash flow and income statements are like looking at the amount of water, "actually" and "imaginary" respectively, pumped in and out of the glass. So, when a corporation starts, it sells shares to whomever.  The amount of cash received is accounted for in the investing section of the cash flow statement under the subheading "issuance (retirement) of stock" or the like, so when shares are sold, it is "issuance"; when a company buys back their shares, it's called "retirement", as cash inflows and outflows respectively. If you had a balance sheet before the shares were sold, you'd see under the "equity" heading a subheading common stock with a nominal (irrelevant) par value (this is usually something obnoxiously low like $0.01 per share used for ease of counting the shares from the Dollar amount in the account) under the subaccount almost always called "common stock".  If you looked at the balance sheet after the sale, you'd see the number of shares in a note to the side. When shares trade publicly, the corporation usually has very little to do with it unless if they are selling or buying new shares under whatever label such as IPO, secondary offering, share repurchase, etc, but the corporation's volume from such activity would still be far below the activity of the third parties: shares are trading almost exclusively between third parties. These share sales and purchases will only be seen on the income statement under earnings per share (EPS), as EPS will rise and fall with stock repurchases and sales assuming income is held constant.  While not technically part of the income statement but printed with it, the "basic weighted average" and "diluted weighted average" number of shares are also printed which are the weighted average over the reporting period of shares actually issued and expected if all promises to issue shares with employee stock options, grants, convertibles were made kept. The income statement is the accrual accounts of the operations of the company.  It has little detail on investing (depreciation & appreciation) or financing (interest expenses & preferred dividends).

Couples are moving again for better job opportunities. They are more likely to make those moves when the husband’s earnings stand to benefit. Men’s earnings increase 5% to 10% after a move, while women’s earnings tend to stagnate, according to a September study of opposite-sex couples led by economist Seema Jayachandran of Princeton University. The study finds that they are more likely to go through with it to improve the man’s earnings—even in cases when the woman’s career stands to benefit more by moving. The cooling job market makes the dinner-table deliberation over a move more challenging. “There’s some psychological pressure to be a supportive wife,” said Henriette Johnsen, who restarted her career after moving from Denmark to England for her husband’s finance job. The relocation penalty for women is a rarely examined factor of why women’s earnings often lag behind men’s. While more women are working than ever before, some of what’s holding them back professionally comes from decisions made inside the household. “This imbalance is a hidden factor that keeps women from advancing as quickly as men in their careers,” Jayachandran said. “It’s rooted in household decisions rather than workplace bias.” Shanika Boyd had to take a $10,000 pay cut after moving from Northern Virginia to Miami for her husband’s new airline job. Her career progress stalled, and after three years getting passed over for promotions, she moved back to Virginia with her son. “If I had stayed, my career wouldn’t have recovered,” she said. The share of job seekers relocating for new positions was up in the first two quarters of 2024 after hitting a record low last year, according to a survey by outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The firm expects relocations to keep rising across all wage levels as fully remote work declines. The share of postings on jobs website Indeed that mention remote or hybrid terms peaked at 10.4% in early 2022 but has since declined to 7.8% at the end of September. Remote job postings in sectors like finance, education and government have been declining, according to ZipRecruiter. Some 26% of men and 15% of women who took new jobs said they were required to relocate, a ZipRecruiter survey from earlier this year found. In some industries, frequent moves are the norm. Military families often relocate every few years, which can disrupt the career of the nonmilitary spouse. Kathryn Zahm, who worked in programs and services for older adults, saw her salary drop more than a third when relocating from Washington, D.C., to San Diego in 2015 for her husband’s military post. To remain competitive, she earned a professional certification and volunteered as a long-term care ombudsman, advocating for the rights and well-being of residents in nursing homes. The experience helped her secure a job with a significant raise when they later moved to Chicago. “I could say, ‘I’ve done this as a volunteer,’ and that gave me an edge,” she said. When the couple relocated again to San Diego in 2021, her Chicago employer allowed her to work remotely, she said. She and her family are now back in the Washington, D.C., area. Limit books are managed by exchanges. If an order is not immediately filled, it is sent to the book.  From there, orders are generally executed on price-time-priority.  The one major exception is the precedence hide-not-slide orders have over earlier placed visible slidden limit orders since unslidden orders are treated like a modification/cancellation. To an exchange, a modification is the same as a cancellation since it charges no fees for placing or canceling orders, only for trades.  The timestamp is reset, and price-time-priority is applied in the same way, so if a modified order isn't immediately filled, it is sent back to the book to be filled in order of price-time-priority.

Time value of money is a concept that recognizes the fact that money today is worth more than the same amount of money in the future. This is because money today can be invested and earn a return, thus increasing its value over time.For example, if you have $100 today and invest it at a 5% annual interest rate, in one year you would have $105. The $5 of additional money is the result of the time value of money, as the $100 was able to earn interest over the course of the year.Compound interest is the interest that is earned on an initial principal and on the accumulated interest of previous periods. This means that the more time that passes, the more interest you will earn, and the faster your money will grow.For example, if you have $100 and earn 5% interest per year, at the end of the first year you would have $105. At the end of the second year, you would earn 5% interest not only on the original $100, but also on the $5 of interest that you earned in the first year. This means that at the end of the second year, you would have $110.25. The $5.25 of additional money is the result of compound interest.Compound interest can be a powerful tool for growing your wealth over time, but it can also work against you if you have debt that is accruing interest. In this case, it is important to pay off your debt as quickly as possible to minimize the amount of interest you will pay.

Squirting cucumbers are not exactly garden celebrities, but these spiky, olive-sized fruits pack a startling defense system: when ripe, they launch their seeds with enough force to startle an unsuspecting passer-by. According to new research, these botanical grenadiers can fling their tiny projectiles nearly 40 feet through the air. And while this phenomenon has been documented by naturalists for centuries, the precise mechanics have remained murky—until now.

The plant at the heart of this high-pressure drama is the squirting cucumber (*Ecballium elaterium*), a species native to the Mediterranean region. It produces small, knobby fruits that, at a glance, look like miniature water balloons draped in fine hairs. But inside each fruit, fluid pressure builds steadily as it matures. At a certain point, the slightest disturbance—such as an animal brushing past or a light gust of wind—causes the fruit to detach from its stem, suddenly releasing an interior slurry of seeds and pulp.

“People have known about squirting cucumbers for centuries,” said Dr. Paolo Ricci, a plant physiologist at the University of Padua in Italy who has studied Mediterranean flora for over a decade. “They appear in old herbal manuscripts, with descriptions of the seeds shooting out like tiny arrows. Yet how they generate such a remarkable force has puzzled botanists.”

In a study published this month in the journal *Interface*, a team of scientists set out to decode the physics behind this explosive seed dispersal. Using high-speed cameras, pressure sensors, and fresh samples grown in test plots near Athens, they recorded the fruits at the exact moment they snapped off their stems. By slowing the footage down to a few thousand frames per second, the researchers observed how the fruit’s internal pressure, built up over days, was channeled into a split-second release.

The key, they found, lies in the cucumber’s internal architecture. Each fruit is essentially a fluid-filled capsule with a thicker rind at the stem end. As water and dissolved sugars accumulate inside, the internal pressure can climb to several times normal atmospheric pressure. This tension is kept in check until a small “weak point” around the stem finally fails. Once that point ruptures, the fruit transforms into a natural water cannon, ejecting seeds at speeds that can top 30 feet per second.

“Think of it like twisting a balloon full of water,” said Dr. Natalia Sideris, an applied biomechanist at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens and an author of the study. “There’s a moment when the force inside just overwhelms the balloon’s skin. With the squirting cucumber, the fruit’s structure and fluid content create this perfect storm of pressure. The instant the stem seals break, everything inside blasts outward.”

The seeds, surrounded by a slimy gel, are propelled far from the parent plant. This is a critical evolutionary advantage: by flinging its offspring across a wide area, the squirting cucumber reduces competition among seedlings and increases the odds that some will sprout in favorable conditions. The mechanism is a vivid example of how plants, despite their sedentary nature, have evolved ingenious strategies to spread their genes.

One surprising revelation came from measuring the angles and trajectories of the seeds. The team found that the fruit’s internal geometry helps direct the seeds in a roughly horizontal spread, not just randomly upward or downward. “We saw this consistent radial pattern,” said Dr. Sideris. “It’s not just an explosion—it’s a controlled blast that maximizes seed distribution.”

The researchers believe that understanding such natural dispersal methods might offer insights into engineering applications—perhaps in designing small-scale devices that harness fluid pressure for precise projectile launches. It’s not the first time botanists have inspired inventors; burrs led to Velcro, and lotus leaves inspired water-repellent coatings. Now, the squirting cucumber may claim a small place in the pantheon of nature’s design innovations.

Still, Dr. Ricci cautions that this research is motivated by curiosity, not commerce. “To me, it’s about appreciating the sheer cleverness of plant evolution,” he said. “We tend to think of plants as passive, but here’s one that’s rigged to go off like a tiny catapult. If you’ve ever doubted the dynamism of the plant kingdom, a face full of cucumber seeds might change your mind.” Without a neat narrative arc or any polite warnings, the squirting cucumber simply does its thing—quietly biding its time until it’s ready to fire.

There are several potential causes of lower back pain that radiates to the buttocks and legs. These can include:

Herniated disc: A herniated disc occurs when the inner gel-like material of a spinal disc pushes out through a tear in the outer layer. This can cause pain, numbness, and weakness in the lower back, buttocks, and legs.

Sciatica: This is a type of pain that occurs when the sciatic nerve, which runs from the lower back through the buttocks and down the legs, becomes compressed or irritated. Sciatica can cause pain, numbness, and tingling in the lower back, buttocks, and legs.

Spinal stenosis: This is a condition in which the spaces within the spine narrow, putting pressure on the spinal cord and nerves. This can cause pain, numbness, and weakness in the lower back, buttocks, and legs.

Piriformis syndrome: The piriformis muscle is located deep in the buttocks. If it becomes tight or inflamed, it can put pressure on the sciatic nerve and cause pain, numbness, and tingling in the lower back, buttocks, and legs.

Muscular strains or sprains: Overuse or injury to the muscles in the lower back, buttocks, or legs can cause pain and discomfort.

It's important to see a healthcare provider for a proper diagnosis and treatment plan. In the meantime, you can try applying heat or cold to the affected area, taking over-the-counter pain medication, and doing gentle stretches to help relieve the pain.

On an ordinary day, beachcombers roaming the rocky shores of Newfoundland can hope to find treasures like mermaid’s purses, barnacle shells and a rainbow’s worth of sea-polished glass fragments. The oddest thing might be the occasional moose teeth, tools or even a doll’s head. 

Weird, white mystery blobs are another matter. 

“It’s the first time I’ve ever seen anything like it, and I’ve lived right here in Placentia Bay my whole life,” said David McGrath, a 67-year-old retiree who stumbled across the mysterious newcomers last month. 

The Canadian Coast Guard was notified. Beaches on the southern shores of the North Atlantic isle were briefly roped off. A federal agency began investigating. 

The blobs range in size from a coin to a dinner plate. They come in an almost pristine white before mixing with sand and turning darker. They are sticky. And they are — this the main thing — indisputably blobby. 

After that, there is some disagreement. 

Some say the blobs carry a whiff of odor not unlike paint. 

But Mr. McGrath said he had not detected that, even when he broke one of them apart with a stick, though that may have been because the air was heavy with the smell of salt. “The ocean was a little frisky at the time,” he said. 

Another beachcomber, Philip Grace, said that he and his wife were walking along the bay last month when they ran across first a scattering of blobs and then many of them. Like Mr. McGrath, he decided to pry one apart. 

“It had a texture similar to not-fully-cooked dough or foam,” Mr. Grace said. More precisely, he said, it resembled the dough used for a Newfoundland fried bread dish called toutons. 

He turned for help to fellow beachcombers online, where people suggested a wide range of possible culprits. They ranged from the industrial (palm oil, paraffin, pollution) to the biological (slime mold, an invertebrate called sea pork and whale excretions). 

Before long, the authorities joined in. 

A federal agency, Environment and Climate Change Canada, said that in the days and weeks after it was notified about the wash-ups on Sept. 7, it sent environmental officers and scientists to collect samples and assess the effects on the shore. The agency said it had also conducted “several aerial, underwater and manual surveys of the beaches and shorelines” to try to ascertain the extent of the spread and its source. 

But mystery still reigns. 

“At this time, neither the substance nor its source has been identified,” the agency said this week. It did say that early tests indicated the blobs might be plant-based. 

Scientists not involved in the investigation said that while there were many tests that could be performed — the ocean has long thrown up mysterious things to puzzle over — it would take time to narrow down the possibilities. 

“There is no one telltale piece of information that’s going to slam-dunk this,” said Christopher Reddy, a senior scientist in marine chemistry and geochemistry at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.  Instead, he said, the mystery might need to be solved through “an ensemble of chemical, biological, physical and geographic data.” 

Another scientist, Steven Carr, a biologist at Memorial University of Newfoundland, said he did not think the material originated from an animal, at least based on the photos. It does not look like ambergris, the sperm whale excretion used in perfumes, he said. Bits of whale carcass would smell far more powerfully. Sea sponges have holes, but not like those found in the blobs. 

Like some of the locals, Mr. Carr also raised the specter of baked-goods incursion, though he cited not toutons but perhaps pastries or pierogies that were abraded by seawater but preserved some shape. But he said that without a sample to examine firsthand, “right now I’m stumped.” 

Until more is known, scientists said, beachgoers should be careful. “If something came to my lab that was a complete unknown, I would have to treat it with a certain cautiousness,” Mr. Reddy said. 

Mr. McGrath, for one, is hoping answers come soon. “We still don’t know if it’s chemical or toxic or harmful to the environment, pets, humans,” he said. 

But mostly he hopes that the blobs, which on Tuesday were still littering the beaches, are gone soon. 

“It’s not very nice,” he said.

Walk along St. Charles Avenue during Carnival season, and you’ll spot a series of towering floats with riders tossing beads and trinkets into the cheering crowd. You may also notice something else: every single person on those floats is masked. This isn’t just tradition—it’s actually required by city ordinance. For all the costumes, music, and king cakes floating around, the mask rule remains one of the few ironclad expectations placed on those who ride.

“Mardi Gras has long been about stepping outside everyday rules,” says Arthur Hardy, publisher of **Arthur Hardy’s Mardi Gras Guide**, who has chronicled the season for decades. “When riders hide their faces, it helps break down social barriers. It’s not about who you are back at the office or how much money you make. Everyone on that float is an equal participant in the fun.”

The masking custom dates back to the 19th century, when members of the earliest krewes—Rex, Proteus, Momus—sought ways to mingle with neighbors without being identified. Masking allowed a well-known judge to stand next to a dockworker without anyone gawking or drawing lines based on station. Today, city rules still demand that every float rider remain masked from start to finish. If you try to flout that requirement, you risk being removed before the parade even begins.

“Mardi Gras was born out of old European masquerade traditions,” explains Dr. Kim Vaz-Deville, a New Orleans scholar who has written extensively about the city’s carnival heritage. “Wearing a mask means you’re free to interact with folks you might never speak to otherwise. It’s one reason the season still feels so refreshing—it shuffles the deck.”

This sense of anonymity is part of what makes Mardi Gras different from other celebrations. In places like Rio de Janeiro or Venice, costumes might be dazzling, but the New Orleans approach makes face coverings a firm rule for those riding the floats. The city takes this seriously enough that officers have, on occasion, reminded krewes to check their riders’ masks before rolling.

Local riders take the custom in stride. “I’ve been on a float in the Krewe of Muses for more than 15 years,” says Sandra Martin, a participant who asked that her last name be used to help preserve her mystique. “I love that no one knows it’s me under there. It’s wild—I can throw beads to my boss or my own cousin, and they have no idea. It levels the field and keeps the spirit of surprise alive.”

The mask rule also helps maintain the carnival’s time-honored mystique. Without it, a parade might feel a bit like a corporate promo or a social club outing. Instead, you get something unpredictable, where everyone—from a local politician to a first-time visitor—stands side by side, catching beads from a stranger whose identity remains hidden behind bright feathers and sequins.

If you find yourself along the parade route, gazing up at the color and chaos, don’t expect to recognize the faces grinning behind those masks. That’s the point. Mardi Gras, at its best, has always invited people to shake off their usual roles and just have a blast—anonymously. The mask keeps that spirit breathing, year after year.

It is possible that the tightness you are experiencing around your chest while eating could be due to a condition called esophageal spasm. Esophageal spasm is a disorder of the muscle contractions in the esophagus, the tube that carries food from the mouth to the stomach. It can cause symptoms such as chest pain, difficulty swallowing, and the feeling of food getting stuck in the throat.

There are several possible causes of esophageal spasm, including acid reflux, a hiatal hernia, and abnormal nerve or muscle function in the esophagus. Consuming hot food may exacerbate the symptoms of esophageal spasm, but it is not the sole cause of the condition.

It is important to discuss your symptoms with a medical professional to determine the cause and appropriate treatment. They may recommend medications or other treatments to help alleviate the symptoms of esophageal spasm. In the meantime, it may be helpful to avoid hot or spicy foods, as well as eating large meals, as these can contribute to the symptoms of the condition.

In cities worldwide, artificial illumination has become such a constant feature of the night sky that many of us no longer notice it. Yet for the creatures that share our planet—and even for the plants that feed them—this perpetual glow is reshaping ancient cycles of life. According to a new study from researchers in China, the subtle glow of streetlights is altering how leaves grow and influencing which creatures find them tasty.

“We’ve long known that artificial light at night can disrupt the behavior of insects, birds, and even some mammals,” says Dr. Xiaoyu Li, a plant ecologist at Zhejiang University and lead author of the study. “But what we found here is that these lights can also change the very fabric of plants’ leaves, modifying them in ways that affect entire food chains.”

**The Changing Leaf Landscape**  
Plants rely on light for photosynthesis, using the sun’s rays to generate energy. Natural day-night cycles also play an essential role in signaling when to grow, reproduce, or shed leaves. Streetlights, with their steady glow, interfere with these signals. Unlike moonlight or the dim glow of starlight, streetlights create a more consistent and intense source of illumination that mimics aspects of daytime—just when the plant’s genes expect darkness.

In the study, which involved comparing leaves from urban environments with a strong presence of artificial light to leaves from more rural, naturally lit areas, researchers identified significant differences in leaf texture and chemical composition. “Leaves growing under constant artificial light tend to develop thicker cuticles,” explains Dr. Li. “This protective layer is like the plant’s natural suit of armor, and when it thickens, it can make the leaves tougher and less palatable to insects.”

**Impacts on Insect Diets**  
At first glance, it might seem like tougher leaves are a good thing for the plants—an extra defensive barrier against hungry herbivores. But nature’s checks and balances are more delicate than that. Insects, including caterpillars and beetles, play a critical role in ecosystems. They break down plant matter, cycle nutrients through the soil, and serve as a key food source for birds, amphibians, and other animals.

When insects find leaves harder to digest, it can have a cascading effect. “If insects struggle to eat and reproduce, the animals that depend on them will also suffer,” says Dr. Wei Zhang, an entomologist at Nanjing Agricultural University, who was not involved in the study but reviewed the findings. “It’s a chain reaction. Changes at the plant level ripple out through entire communities.”

**Artificial Light’s Domino Effect**  
One of the intriguing parts of the research is how subtly and indirectly streetlights are altering these ecosystems. Artificial light doesn’t just extend the daytime; it can also alter a plant’s internal clock, known as the circadian rhythm. A disrupted circadian rhythm can lead to changes in when leaves are produced, how thick they grow, and even the levels of certain defensive chemicals, like tannins. These chemicals not only deter insects but can also influence nutrient cycling in the soil when the leaves eventually fall.

Insects, for their part, have also been known to respond to light pollution in multiple ways. Some are drawn toward it—like moths circling a lamp—while others avoid well-lit areas. Over time, this can rearrange the distribution of insect species within a city or region. “It’s not just a single effect,” says Dr. Zhang. “We’re looking at a mesh of interconnected relationships. The light changes the leaves, the leaves change the insects’ diets, and the altered insect populations then affect predators and the overall ecological balance.”

**Global Implications**  
What makes this discovery especially significant is the global scale of light pollution. According to the International Dark-Sky Association, light pollution grows at a rate of around two percent per year globally. As more people move into urban areas, artificial lighting expands. From suburban neighborhoods to city centers, streetlights, billboard lamps, and even ambient building lights create a haze that’s visible for miles.

“This research from China highlights a crucial but often overlooked dimension of environmental change,” says Dr. Linda Gregg, a conservation biologist at the University of British Columbia. “We talk a lot about habitat destruction, climate change, and pollution. Artificial light is a form of pollution, too—just less visible in its immediate consequences. We’re starting to understand that it can directly impact plant-insect interactions, which are at the heart of terrestrial ecosystems.”

**Conservation and Mitigation**  
So, what can be done to minimize these unintended consequences? Experts suggest a range of strategies. Simple interventions might include using lower-intensity bulbs, directing light downward rather than outward and upward, and employing motion sensors or timers so that lights are used only when needed. Switching from blue-white LED lights to warmer tones may also help, as research suggests that some wavelengths of light are less disruptive to wildlife.

“Urban planners and policymakers can take note,” says Dr. Gregg. “The design of our cities shouldn’t only consider human comfort and safety—though that’s certainly important—but also the well-being of other species. If we can reduce unnecessary light at night, we can help restore some balance.”

**A Growing Field of Study**  
While this research offers important insights, it also raises new questions. Will certain types of trees be more affected than others? How will different insect species adapt or fail to adapt? And what long-term impacts might this have on urban ecosystems? The authors of the study hope their findings inspire more research, as well as dialogue among ecologists, city planners, and the public.

“There’s so much more to learn,” says Dr. Li. “But one thing is clear: The changes we make to our environment—like installing more streetlights—do not just affect humans. They shape the world for countless other living things. As we illuminate our streets, we also change the fate of leaves, insects, and all the life that depends on them. We need to be thoughtful custodians of this planet, especially as our cities continue to expand.”

In this era of constant human-driven change, it turns out that streetlights are not just guiding our way home—they’re also quietly rewriting the recipes of life on Earth.

Oddly enough, in the USA, there are enough cost and tax savings between buy-and-hold of a static portfolio and buying into a fund that a few brokerages have sprung up around the concept, such as FolioFN, to make it easier for small investors to manage numerous small holdings via fractional shares and no commission window trades. A static buy-and-hold portfolio of stocks can be had for a few dollars per trade.  Buying into a fund involves various annual and one time fees that are quoted as percentages of the investment.  Even 1-2% can be a lot, especially if it is every year.  Typically, a US mutual fund must send out a 1099 tax form to each investor, stating that investors share of the dividends and capital gains for each year. The true impact of this is not obvious until you get a tax bill for gains that you did not enjoy, which can happen when you buy into a fund late in the year that has realized capital gains.  What fund investors sometimes fail to appreciate is that they are taxed both on their own holding period of fund shares and the fund's capital gains distributions determined by the fund's holding period of its investments. For example, if ABC tech fund bought Google stock several years ago for $100/share, and sold it for $500/share in the same year you bought into the ABC fund, then you will receive a "capital gains distribution" on your 1099 that will include some dollar amount, which is considered your share of that long-term profit for tax purposes. The amount is not customized for your holding period, capital gains are distributed pro-rata among all current fund shareholders as of the ex-distribution date. Morningstar tracks this as Potential Capital Gains Exposure and so there is a way to check this possibility before investing. Funds who have unsold losers in their portfolio are also affected by these same rules, have been called "free rides" because those funds, if they find some winners, will have losers that they can sell simultaneously with the winners to remain tax neutral.  See "On the Lookout for Tax Traps and Free Riders", Morningstar, pdf In contrast, buying-and-holding a portfolio does not attract any capital gains taxes until the stocks in the portfolio are sold at a profit.  A fund often is actively managed.  That is, experts will alter the portfolio from time to time or advise the fund to buy or sell particular investments. Note however, that even the experts are required to tell you that "past performance is no guarantee of future results."

The Australian government announced on Thursday that it plans to ban children under the age of 16 from using social media, introducing what officials describe as “world-leading” legislation. Under the proposed laws, social media platforms will be required to verify the ages of their users and ensure that no one below the age of 16 creates or maintains an account. Companies that fail to comply with these measures may face stiff penalties, including significant fines or even being blocked within the country.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the new regulations are designed to address growing concerns about the impact of social media on the mental health and development of young Australians. “We owe it to our children to protect them from harmful online content and to give parents peace of mind,” Albanese stated at a press conference in Canberra. “This legislation is about setting a clear standard: if you’re too young to drive a car or buy alcohol, you’re certainly too young to navigate the adult world of social media without robust safeguards.”

**Why Now?**  
The proposed age limit comes amid increasing global debate about online safety and the responsibilities of major technology companies to protect younger users. The Australian government pointed to rising rates of cyberbullying, exposure to inappropriate content, and personal data collection from young users as key motivating factors. According to a 2023 study by the Australian Institute of Family Studies, more than half of children aged 10 to 15 have some form of social media presence, often without parental knowledge or supervision.

“Children are joining these platforms at increasingly younger ages,” said Dr. Helen Carter, a child psychologist at the University of Sydney. “This exposes them to a host of risks—lower self-esteem due to unrealistic body images, anxiety and depression triggered by online bullying, and potentially harmful interactions with strangers.” Carter believes that setting an age limit is a step in the right direction. “We regulate so many other aspects of a child’s environment—schooling, medical care, nutrition. It makes sense to also regulate their digital life, which is becoming a huge part of their world.”

**How Will It Work?**  
Ensuring compliance will likely prove challenging. Under the proposed regulations, social media platforms—such as Facebook, Instagram, Snapchat, TikTok, and emerging newcomers—must implement effective age verification methods. This could range from verifying government-issued identification to using advanced age estimation technology, such as artificial intelligence tools that analyze user activity.

“We understand this will not be simple,” said Technology Minister Ed Henshaw, who drafted the bill. “But these companies have the resources and the know-how to innovate. We’re asking them to do what they do best: use technology to solve complex problems. If they can personalize ads and content with pinpoint accuracy, they can figure out how old their users are.”

Platform operators that fail to remove underage users could face large fines or even have their services suspended in Australia. The government has not specified exact penalty amounts yet, but Henshaw hinted that fines could be “substantially higher” than existing penalties for data breaches.

**Industry Reactions**  
Social media platforms have responded with a mix of caution and concern. Many companies argue that determining the exact age of a user, especially if that user is motivated to hide their true age, is a complex task. Some worry that strict verification procedures might discourage legitimate users, cause privacy concerns, or be easily circumvented by tech-savvy minors.

“While we support efforts to keep young people safe, we need to be mindful of users’ privacy and their right to online access,” said Danielle Wright, a spokesperson for the Association of Social Media Platforms, an industry group representing major global companies. “We are eager to collaborate with the Australian government to develop practical and effective solutions, but we must ensure that these measures don’t backfire or set impossible standards.”

**Balancing Privacy and Protection**  
Critics of the legislation worry about the privacy implications of the new rules. For effective age verification, platforms may need to collect more personal information, raising questions about who will have access to that data and how securely it will be stored.

Digital rights advocates warn that without proper checks, the new requirements could create unintended consequences. “We understand the government’s motive, but we must avoid creating a surveillance-heavy online environment,” said Ingrid Thompson, policy director at Digital Rights Australia. “If platforms start requiring IDs or other sensitive documents from users, not only children but adults too could face potential privacy violations. The solution must be as sophisticated as the problem.”

**A Global Trend?**  
Australia’s proposed legislation comes at a time when countries around the world are wrestling with similar issues. The United Kingdom, for instance, recently updated its Online Safety Bill with provisions aimed at protecting children from harmful content. In the United States, several state legislatures have introduced bills mandating parental consent for minors to join social media.

International observers say Australia’s approach could set a powerful precedent. “What Australia is doing may very well spur other countries to follow suit,” said Dr. Martin Koller, a media regulation expert at the European Centre for Digital Policy. “If large platforms adapt their systems for Australia, it could be simpler for them to roll out similar measures in other jurisdictions. This could lead to a global push for stricter age controls online.”

**Looking Ahead**  
The legislation is expected to go before the Australian Parliament later this year, with debates likely focusing on practical implementation and the balance between protection and privacy. If passed, platforms will be given a grace period to comply.

For many parents, the new rules can’t come soon enough. “I’m always worried about what my daughter might stumble across online,” said Sydney resident Marissa Boyle, mother of a 14-year-old. “If a rule like this can help keep her safe, I’m all for it.”

While the road ahead is uncertain, the Australian government’s move reflects a growing consensus that the digital world needs clearer rules when it comes to children. As other nations watch closely, the age limit proposal might herald a new era of globally recognized online standards for young users, ensuring that the internet’s youngest citizens can explore it safely and responsibly.

Before the English Restoration, audiences in London’s playhouses might see kings, fools, gods, or devils, but never an actual woman earning her living on the public stage. Men and boys took every role, fashioning elaborate costumes and falsettos to portray queens, young maidens, and even nuns. This convention held for generations—until December 8, 1660, when a woman stepped forward under the stage lights, performed for a paying crowd, and changed English theater’s course. Even now, more than 360 years later, we cannot say with absolute certainty who she was.

Many scholars argue the actress was Margaret Hughes, who is recorded as having played Desdemona in a production of **Othello** staged by the King’s Company at the Vere Street Theatre. Others suggest it might have been Anne Marshall or a different performer whose name has slipped into obscurity. Regardless, this mysterious debutant has become a legendary figure, ushering in a new era of professional female performers—a development unimaginable during the strictly all-male traditions of Elizabethan and Jacobean drama.

Dr. Clare McManus, an early modern theater historian at the University of Roehampton, reflects on the uncertainty. “We know a play was performed, we know it included a woman in a female role for the first time on the English public stage, and we know that many eyewitnesses were stunned,” she says. “The problem is the historical record doesn’t always give us a tidy name. This fog of ambiguity leaves room for debate—and that debate has persisted since the 17th century.”

In his diary, Samuel Pepys never quite pinned down this actress’s identity, though he did remark on seeing women perform around that time. Other observers wrote of their surprise and delight, marveling at the novelty of seeing a genuine woman’s face where, just months earlier, only painted boys had stood. Charles II’s court had recently reestablished the monarchy, and the king’s fascination with Continental styles of theater—where women had already been performing—likely played a role in encouraging this shift.

Before long, the presence of female performers no longer shocked playgoers. Actresses such as Nell Gwyn, Elizabeth Barry, and Anne Bracegirdle became major attractions in London’s bustling theaters. Yet, McManus notes that this initial breakthrough moment is still overshadowed by the namelessness of its principal pioneer. “It’s ironic that the actress who opened the door remains a shadowy figure,” she says. “We celebrate this watershed day, but we’re forced to rely on fragments of evidence. In truth, no single playbill or letter clearly states her identity.”

Contemporary writers often described the first professional English actress as daring simply for appearing in public—a striking shift in an era when women’s voices and bodies had been policed and restricted. Soon after 1660, audiences grew accustomed to seeing actresses in tragic roles, witty heroines, and even breeches parts (women dressed as men). Ticket sales soared. Playwrights adapted their scripts to better suit female performers, introducing complex female characters who could be convincingly portrayed by women rather than by teenage boys.

Over time, the anonymous figure behind that first public performance became both a symbol of freedom and a riddle historians continue to puzzle over. We have signatures on later contracts, memoirs that mention famous actresses, paintings that depict 17th-century stage luminaries—but the exact name of the woman who broke that barrier on a December evening in 1660 refuses to come into clear focus.

“The original records were never meant to serve as a neat origin story,” McManus observes. “They were day-to-day notes and casual remarks. People were excited, but not always careful in giving us the details we crave now.”

So we remember the event itself: one performance, one woman standing where no English woman had publicly stood before. She altered the sound, sight, and spirit of the stage. While we might never assign her the certainty of a name, the moment she claimed a spot under the stage’s glare still resonates every time an actress steps into the spotlight.

The impact of this phenomenon extends beyond aesthetic concerns. The mountain's snowpack plays a crucial role in the local ecosystem and water supply, feeding springs and rivers that support agriculture and industry in the surrounding regions.

"The reduced snowfall and later onset of winter conditions could have cascading effects on local water resources and agricultural patterns," warns Dr. Sarah Chen, an environmental scientist at the International Climate Research Institute. The situation at Mount Fuji mirrors similar trends observed at other mountains across Japan, where warming temperatures have led to shorter snow seasons and reduced snowfall. This pattern has implications for the country's winter tourism industry and traditional winter activities.

Looking ahead, climate scientists predict that such anomalies might become more common. "While we can't attribute any single weather event directly to climate change, the delayed snowfall at Mount Fuji is consistent with what climate models predict for a warming world," explains Dr. Yamamoto.

The mountain's delayed snowfall adds to the growing list of climate-related anomalies observed worldwide, highlighting the need for continued environmental monitoring and climate action.

The question now facing scientists and local communities is whether this year's delayed snowfall represents an outlier or a new normal for Japan's beloved mountain. No, you do not need an OCI card to continue to have an NRE or NRO account. But, you should inform the banks where you have NRE and NRO accounts that you have changed citizenship, and they may need to go through their KYC (Know Your Customer) process with you all over again.  If you don't get an OCI Card, you will need to have an Indian visa stamped into your new US passport to visit India, and please do remember to send your Indian passport to the nearest Indian Consulate for cancellation. Keep the surrender certificate and cancelled passport in your safe deposit box forever; your grandchildren will need it to get visas to visit India. (My granddaughter just did). If you do get an OCI Card, you will need to have an OCI stamp put into your new US passport, and when you renew your US passport, you will need to get the new one stamped too (and pay the fee for that, of course). You cannot enter India with just an OCI Card and a US passport without the OCI stamp in it; that stamp is vital. If you move from one residential address in the US to another,  you will need to  get a new OCI Card issued because, unlike the US "green card", the OCI card has your residential address on it. Once again, a fee is involved.  All these processes take many weeks because the whole paperwork has to go to the Ministry of External Affairs in New Delhi, and meanwhile, your passport is not available to you for a trip to Europe or Japan or Taiwan or China if you need to go there on business (or for pleasure).

As others have said, please talk to a professional adviser. From my quick research, domain names can only be amortized as 197 intangible if it's used for the taxpayer's business. For example, if Corp A pays $200,000 for corpa.com and uses that to point to their homepage, they can amortize it over 15 years as a 197 intangible. (Please refer to this IRS memo https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-wd/201543014.pdf.) The above memo does not issue any guidance in your case, where domains are purchased for investment or resale. Regarding domain names, the U.S. Master Depreciation Guide (2016) by CCH says: Many domain names are purchased in a secondary market from third parties [...] who register names and resell them at a profit. These cost must be capitalized because the name will have a useful   life of more than one year. The costs cannot be amortized because a   domain name has no useful life. So your decision to capitalize is correct, but your amortization deductions may be challenged by the IRS. When you sell your domain, the gain will be determined by how you treat these assets. If you treat your domains as 197 intangibles, and thus had ordinary deductions through amortization, your gain will be ordinary. If you treated them as capital assets, your gain will be a capital gain. Very conceptually, and because the IRS has not issued specific guidelines, I think holding domain names for resale is similar to buying stock of a company. You can't amortize the investment, and when you sell, the gain or loss is a capital gain/loss.

Friday the 13th has long been considered an unlucky day, a superstition that has permeated cultures around the world. But how did this date earn its ominous reputation, and why does it continue to influence even those who claim not to believe in superstitions? To understand the roots of this fear, we must delve into history, psychology, and cultural phenomena.

The fear of the number 13, known as triskaidekaphobia, is a key component of the superstition surrounding Friday the 13th. According to Dr. Stuart Vyse, a psychologist and author of "Believing in Magic: The Psychology of Superstition," the number 13 has been considered unlucky for centuries. "The number 12 is often seen as a 'complete' number," Vyse explains. "There are 12 months in a year, 12 zodiac signs, 12 apostles of Jesus, and so on. The number 13, by contrast, is seen as irregular and thus carries a sense of foreboding."

The specific fear of Friday the 13th, however, is a more recent development. Many historians trace its origins to the late 19th and early 20th centuries. One popular theory links it to the Knights Templar, a medieval Christian military order. On Friday, October 13, 1307, King Philip IV of France ordered the arrest of hundreds of Templars, leading to their torture and execution. This event, though not widely associated with the superstition until much later, is often cited as a historical basis for the fear.

Another contributing factor is the publication of Thomas W. Lawson's novel "Friday, the Thirteenth" in 1907. The book tells the story of a stockbroker who uses the superstition to create chaos on Wall Street. "Lawson's novel helped cement the idea of Friday the 13th as a day of misfortune in the public consciousness," says Dr. Donald Dossey, a folklore historian and author of "Holiday Folklore, Phobias and Fun."

Despite its murky origins, the fear of Friday the 13th has real-world implications. Studies have shown that many people alter their behavior on this day, avoiding travel, major purchases, or important decisions. The Stress Management Center and Phobia Institute estimates that businesses in the United States lose between $700 million and $800 million on Friday the 13th due to decreased economic activity.

Interestingly, even those who claim not to believe in superstitions can be influenced by them. This phenomenon is known as the "nocebo effect," where negative expectations lead to negative outcomes. "If you expect something bad to happen, you might unconsciously behave in ways that make it more likely," explains Dr. Vyse. "It's a self-fulfilling prophecy."

Cultural reinforcement also plays a significant role. Movies like the "Friday the 13th" horror franchise have perpetuated the idea of the date as a harbinger of doom. "Media representations can amplify and sustain superstitions," says Dr. Dossey. "They create a feedback loop where the superstition is both a source of entertainment and a genuine source of anxiety."

Despite its reputation, Friday the 13th is not universally feared. In some cultures, the number 13 is considered lucky. For example, in Italy, the number 17 is seen as unlucky, while 13 is often associated with good fortune. This cultural variability highlights the arbitrary nature of superstitions and their reliance on social context.

In conclusion, the fear of Friday the 13th is a complex interplay of historical events, psychological tendencies, and cultural narratives. While it may seem irrational, the superstition continues to hold sway over many, influencing behavior and perceptions in subtle yet significant ways. As Dr. Vyse aptly puts it, "Superstitions are a testament to the power of human imagination and the ways in which we seek to make sense of an unpredictable world." Whether you choose to embrace or dismiss the superstition, Friday the 13th remains a fascinating example of how collective beliefs can shape our reality.

Exposure is the amount of money that you are at risk of losing on a given position (i.e. on a UST 10 year bond), portfolio of positions, strategy (selling covered calls for example), or counterparty, usually represented as a percentage of your total assets. Interbank exposure is the exposure of banks to other banks either through owning debt or stock, or by having open positions with the other banks as counterparties. Leveraging occurs when the value of your position is more than the value of what you are trading in. One example of this is borrowing money (i.e. creating debt for yourself) to buy bonds. The amount of your own funds that you are using to pay for the position is "leveraged" by the debt so that you are risking more than 100% of your capital if, for example, the bond became worthless). Another example would be buying futures "on margin" where you only put up the margin value of the trade and not the full cost. The problem with these leveraged positions is what happens if a credit event (default etc.) happens. Since a large amount of the leverage is being "passed on" as banks are issuing debt to buy other banks' debt who are issuing debt to buy debt there is a risk that a single failure could cause an unravelling of these leveraged positions and, since the prices of the bonds will be falling resulting in these leveraged positions losing money, it will cause a cascade of losses and defaults. If a leveraged position becomes worth less than the amount of real (rather than borrowed or margined) money that was put up to take the position then it is almost inevitable that the firm in that position will default on the requirements for the leverage. You said your strategy was to put it into a index fund.  But then you asked about setting  stock limits.   I'm confused. Funds usually trade at their price at the end of the day, so you shouldn't try to time this at all. Just place your order. If you are buying ETFs, there is going to be so much volume on the market that your small trade is going to have no impact on the price. You should just place a market order. A market order is an order to buy or   sell a stock at the current market   price. A limit order is an order to buy or   sell a security at a specific price. In the US, when you place a trade with any broker, you can either place a limit order or a market order.  A market order just fills your order with the next best sellers in line.  If you place an order for 100 shares, the sellers willing to sell 100 shares at the lowest price will be matched with your order (sometimes you may get 50 shares at one price and 50 shares at a slightly different price).    If your stock has a lot of volatility and you place a market order for a small amount of shares,  you will get the best price. If you place a limit order, you specify the price at which you want to buy shares.  Your order will then only be filled with sellers willing to sell at that price or lower (i.e. they must be at least as good as you specified).  This means you could place an order at a limit that does not get filled (the stock could move in a direction away from your limit price).  If you really want to own the stock, you shouldn't use a limit order.  You shouldn't only use a limit order if you want to tell your broker "I will only buy this stock at this price or better."  p.s. Every day that passes is NOT a waste.  It's just a day that you've decided investing in cash is safer than investing in the market.
