Deep in the heart of the Tarim Basin, an arid desert region in what is now northwestern China, archaeologists made a startling discovery more than a century ago: remarkably well-preserved mummies dating back roughly 3,600 years. These Bronze Age people were found buried with tiny hunks of cheese draped around their necks—a culinary curiosity that has puzzled experts for decades. Now, thanks to advanced DNA analysis, scientists are beginning to understand exactly what was in the world’s oldest known cheese, and why it was placed so close to the deceased.

“Initially, we were astonished by the preservation,” says Dr. Yimin Yang, a bioarchaeologist at the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences who worked on the research. “It’s not every day you find 3,600-year-old dairy products, let alone something as recognizable and intact as cheese.”

For years, historians and archaeologists have speculated about how Bronze Age communities living in the harsh desert environment of the Tarim Basin produced and consumed dairy. The discovery of cheese on these mummies has long suggested that cheesemaking was well-established in the region, potentially as part of funerary rituals or as a way to provide nourishment for the afterlife. But the exact recipe and the origins of this ancient cheese remained elusive—until now.

The research team turned to cutting-edge genetic analysis to unlock the secrets hidden in these tiny cheese lumps. By extracting DNA fragments from the dairy residues, they identified patterns suggesting the use of a fermentation process remarkably similar to that which produces kefir today. This indicates that the Bronze Age cheesemakers weren’t simply curdling milk into a crude lump; they had a sophisticated method for turning milk into a stable, easily digestible food product that could withstand desert conditions.

“We found evidence of lactose-fermenting microorganisms,” explains Dr. Jessica Hendy, a food archaeologist at the University of York who was not involved in the study but has reviewed the findings. “These microbes would have converted the milk sugars, making the cheese more digestible—an important advantage in a world where many adults were lactose intolerant.”

This step toward lactose-free dairy is a significant clue about how ancient societies managed their food supplies and diversified their diets. Cheesemaking likely enabled them to store valuable nutrients for longer periods, a critical adaptation in harsh environments. The Tarim Basin’s uniquely dry, salty conditions appear to have naturally freeze-dried these cheese lumps, perfectly preserving them through millennia.

The DNA evidence suggests that the cheese likely came from a mixture of milks—possibly from goats, sheep, or cattle—and involved complex microbial communities. “We’re seeing a direct link between ancient and modern fermentation practices,” says Dr. Yang. “This points to very old and well-developed traditions of dairy production that stretch across continents and thousands of years.”

The presence of cheese in these burials also hints at cultural or religious significance. Perhaps cheese was believed to sustain the soul in the afterlife or to symbolize prosperity and abundance. While we may never fully understand why the Tarim Basin mummies wore these morsels around their necks, the new findings provide fresh insight into their daily lives, their diets, and their advanced food-processing technologies.

“It’s a remarkable window into the past,” says Dr. Hendy. “By examining something as simple and familiar as cheese, we’re reconnecting with the lived experiences of ancient peoples. We’re reminded that these ancestors, though separated from us by thousands of years, shared our basic need to eat well and prepare for the uncertainties of life—and death.”

In the end, these tiny hunks of ancient cheese teach us that food is never just food; it’s culture, innovation, and tradition, carefully passed down through the ages—and sometimes preserved, astonishingly, for millennia.

We asked a veteran mail carrier to explain what those paw-print stickers mean—and how pet owners can help protect postal workers from dog bites If there’s one thing that Tara Snyder, a veteran mail carrier for the U.S. Postal Service, teaches every new mail carrier she trains, it’s this: “Even if a dog is friendly to you 364 days a year, they can have a bad day too—and bite you. If they have teeth, they can bite.” She knows of what she speaks. In April 2024, Snyder was doing her usual route in Pennsylvania when she approached a resident’s door to get a signature for a piece of mail. Before she realized what was happening, a 70-pound dog launched out the door and went right for her hand. She tried to block it with her mailbag, but it was too late. “It ripped my hand open pretty bad,” she says, noting that she ended up needing 17 stitches, a tetanus shot, a round of antibiotics and three weeks off work to recover. “The worst part was that it bit my right hand, and I’m right-handed.” It wasn’t the first or last confrontation between a mail carrier and a vicious dog at that address. In fact, a different dog cornered Snyder on the porch during a separate visit. (Thankfully, she wasn’t bitten that time.) Animal Control is looking into the owners, and the Postal Service is doing everything it can to stop its mail carriers from getting bitten. Because the fact is, Snyder is not alone: There were 5,800 incidents involving dogs and postal workers in 2023, according to Postal Service data. That brings us to the colored paw-print stickers you may have spotted on mailboxes. Ahead, we’ll explain their meaning, the replacement system that’s keeping mail carriers safe and what you can do if you’re a dog owner. The Paws mailbox sticker program In 2020, the Postal Service rolled out the Paws Program in select cities around the country. Workers placed paw-print stickers on the mailboxes of homes known to have dogs: an orange sticker to indicate that a dog lives at that address and a yellow sticker to signal that a dog lives next door. The goal was to let Postal Service workers and other delivery people know they should be on the lookout for dogs or other animals at that address—especially dogs who don’t react well to mail carriers. The program is no longer active, though you may still spy the stickers on some mailboxes. If you see one on someone else’s mailbox, leave it where it is and take it as a sign that a dog may live there. If you see a sticker on your own mailbox, you can either leave it or remove it. The new Postal Service dog-alert system “The Postal Service has pivoted away from the sticker-based Paw Program and implemented a digital and more effective, sustainable method for alerting letter carriers of potential dangers,” says Amy Gibbs, a spokesperson for the service. That’s right: Your mail carriers have gone high-tech. The same scanner they use on packages now customizes warnings to the exact location, time and situation of individual postal workers. “To help protect our employees, the hand-held scanners used by our carriers to confirm customer delivery include a feature to indicate the presence of a dog at an address,” Gibbs explains. “And the USPS Informed Delivery service alerts customers to mail and packages coming to their homes, allowing them to plan for the carrier’s arrival and secure their dogs safely.” Snyder loves the new program—it’s part of the National Dog Bite Awareness Campaign—as it can alert mail carriers about all kinds of dangers and provide updates on the go. The only downside of the digital system for her: “It doesn’t help other delivery people, like DoorDash drivers or FedEx, and I don’t know if they have a similar warning system,” she says. “I am such an animal lover, and I never want to have anything bad happen to a dog,” Snyder says. “Preventing animal attacks is the best way to protect us and your dog. And don’t say, ‘My dog would never.’ Because any dog can bite under the wrong circumstances.” The No. 1 tip for preventing your dog from biting a mail carrier? “Secure your dog,” both Snyder and Gibbs say. This starts with putting your dog inside when you know the mail carrier is coming, but it doesn’t stop there. “Be aware of what your dog can do,” Snyder says. “Many dogs can open latch doors by jumping on the handle, leap over fences or gates, or barrel through screen doors if they feel threatened. You may need to add extra locks.” Other tips for dog owners: • Tell your mail carrier ahead of time about your dog. • Don’t allow your dog to roam freely. • Fence in your yard, and put your mailbox outside the fence. • Use Informed Delivery (it’s a free service!) for packages that need to be brought to your door. • Don’t allow children to accept mail directly from the carrier, as the dog may become protective of the child. • Keep your dog current on its vaccines, including rabies. • Ensure your dog is covered under your homeowners or renters insurance policy. That last one is important. Many people don’t realize that they will be held personally responsible for the medical bills, lost wages and uniform-replacement costs associated with their dog biting a mail carrier, Gibbs says. The Postal Service takes steps to educate and equip their workers to prevent animal bites, but at the end of the day, the responsibility is on the pet owner, Gibbs says. One of the things your mail carrier may not tell you? If you don’t or can’t secure your dog, you may not be able to have your mail delivered anymore. “If a carrier feels threatened by a vicious dog, or if a dog is running loose, we may ask the owner to pick up their mail at the post office,” she says.

In the pursuit of improved health, the solution could be as straightforward as incorporating more colorful foods into your meals. These compounds play a vital role in a balanced diet, enhancing immunity and combating diseases.

Phytochemicals are naturally occurring substances in plants that offer protective benefits or help prevent diseases. While not essential nutrients like vitamins and minerals, they can significantly influence health. Rachel E. Scherr, a nutrition specialist, describes phytochemicals as nature's method of equipping us with a protective mechanism. They collaborate with other nutrients to enhance health and ward off illnesses.

The idea of "eating the rainbow" is an easy and efficient way to make sure you're consuming a variety of these health-promoting compounds. Every hue found in fruits and vegetables signifies distinct phytochemicals, each offering specific health advantages. For example, the red color in tomatoes and watermelon is due to lycopene, a potent antioxidant associated with a lower risk of some types of cancer. Fruits and vegetables that are orange and yellow, such as carrots and sweet potatoes, are high in beta-carotene, which aids in maintaining eye health and strengthening the immune system.

Leafy greens like spinach and broccoli are rich in lutein and zeaxanthin, compounds that support eye health and might lower the risk of long-term illnesses. Foods that are blue and purple, such as blueberries and eggplants, are rich in anthocyanins, which have been demonstrated to enhance heart health and brain function. White and brown foods, like garlic and mushrooms, are rich in allicin and other substances that possess anti-inflammatory and immune-enhancing qualities.

"Scherr explains that eating a diverse array of colors provides you with a broad spectrum of phytochemicals and helps maintain a balanced intake of vital nutrients." "Having a variety of these foods is crucial for sustaining good health and avoiding nutrient shortages."

Studies indicate that consuming a diet abundant in fruits and vegetables is linked to a reduced risk of chronic illnesses, such as heart disease, diabetes, and some types of cancer. These protective benefits are largely attributed to the role of phytochemicals. They function as antioxidants by neutralizing damaging free radicals in the body and possess anti-inflammatory effects that can lower the risk of chronic inflammation, which is a known factor in many diseases.

Additionally, phytochemicals can boost the immune system, improving its ability to combat infections. They can also affect hormonal balance and mend DNA damage, enhancing their ability to fight diseases.

Adding an assortment of colorful fruits and vegetables to your meals can be simple. Small adjustments, such as incorporating berries into your morning meal, munching on carrot sticks, or having a side salad with your dinner, can have a substantial impact. "Scherr suggests that the essential step is to turn it into a routine." "Begin by introducing one or two new colors to your dishes each week and slowly expand the range."

Experts concur that obtaining phytochemicals from whole foods is preferable, even though supplements are an option. Whole foods offer a rich combination of nutrients that synergize to improve health, a benefit that isolated supplements cannot match.

To sum up, consuming a variety of colorful fruits and vegetables is a tasty and efficient method to tap into the benefits of phytochemicals. This approach can enhance your immune system, combat illnesses, and elevate your general health. The IRS defines “startup costs” as deductible capital expenses that are used to pay for: 1) The cost of “investigating the creation or acquisition of an active trade or business.” This includes costs incurred for surveying markets, product analysis, labor supply, visiting potential business locations and similar expenditures. 2) The cost of getting a business ready to operate (before you open your doors or start generating income). If you're a sole proprietor for tax purposes, then you'll deduct them on Schedule C of your Form 1040 on your personal tax.  If you are a partnership, C-Corp, or S-Corp, they will be accounted at the business level and either passed on to you on a Schedule K (partnership and S-Corp) or deducted directly by the company (C-Corp). In any case, you will need good records that justify your expenses as business related. For most of us, earthquakes are the sudden jolts we feel beneath our feet—unexpected, alarming, and sometimes devastating. But the majority of seismic events that occur on our planet are quiet and subtle, never rattling dishes or causing buildings to sway. These “microquakes” often go unnoticed by human senses and even by many conventional monitoring systems. Yet, hidden within these faint tremors may lie important clues about where and when the next major earthquake—the so-called “Big One”—could strike.

Now, cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) tools are helping scientists sift through vast amounts of seismic data, uncovering patterns that were previously invisible. By training machine-learning algorithms to listen closely to the Earth’s deep rumblings, researchers hope to pinpoint early warning signs of a massive quake, potentially buying valuable time for communities in harm’s way.

**Turning Noise into Knowledge**  
Seismologists have long relied on networks of sensors—called seismometers—to record the vibrations traveling through Earth’s crust. But these recordings can be riddled with noise, from ocean waves pounding distant shores to the hum of human activity. Sorting out meaningful seismic signals from this background chatter is a significant challenge. Traditional methods can miss very faint quakes, especially those that don’t produce the sharp, easily identifiable waves we associate with a strong earthquake.

“AI really excels at pattern recognition,” said Dr. Gregory Beroza, a seismologist at Stanford University. “When you feed these algorithms enough data, they can learn to pick out subtle signals that a human or even standard software might overlook.” With machine learning, what once seemed like random static can reveal swarms of tiny earthquakes, slow-slip events (where tectonic plates gradually grind against each other), and other geological oddities that could be key to forecasting larger quakes.

**From Hidden Quakes to Big-Quake Clues**  
Among the most intriguing discoveries AI has facilitated is the detection of “slow earthquakes.” Unlike the sudden jolts we typically associate with quakes, slow earthquakes unfold over days or weeks, with tectonic plates grinding past each other in slow motion. These events are often too gradual for humans to feel and can be overshadowed by constant seismic noise. Still, they play a vital role in releasing stress along faults.

“Think of a tectonic plate boundary like a stuck zipper,” explained Dr. Heidi Houston, a geophysicist at the University of Southern California. “Big earthquakes are when the zipper suddenly rips open, releasing energy all at once. Slow earthquakes, on the other hand, are like gently tugging at the zipper, gradually easing some tension. The question is how these two processes interact and whether tracking slow events can help us anticipate when a big, catastrophic rupture might occur.”

By scanning seismic data with AI tools, researchers have identified slow-slip events in regions like the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest. Cascadia is known for producing gigantic earthquakes—potentially reaching magnitudes of 9.0 or more. Detecting slow quakes here could shed light on the warning signs that precede a megaquake.

**Training the Machines**  
The process of teaching AI to detect these elusive events begins with feeding it enormous amounts of seismic data. Engineers and seismologists annotate recordings, identifying known earthquakes and labeling background noise. Over time, the algorithm “learns” the difference. Once trained, the AI can process new, unlabeled data and pick out signals far too subtle for a human eye or conventional techniques.

“Machine learning has supercharged our ability to parse through massive datasets,” said Dr. Yunjie Wen, a data scientist working with the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS). “With thousands of seismic stations around the world, we’re talking about a firehose of information. Without AI, it’s like searching for a whisper in a crowded stadium.”

Using a neural network—a type of AI inspired by the structure of the human brain—researchers can even teach the system to distinguish between various types of seismic signals. Over time, these networks become increasingly adept at flagging activity that might hint at changes deep underground.

**Early Warning, Not Crystal Balls**  
While AI offers new ways to detect tiny tremors and better understand earthquake physics, it’s important to remember that predicting exactly when and where a massive quake will hit remains beyond our grasp. Earth is too complex, and earthquakes depend on countless variables. But what AI can do is improve our odds of spotting early warning signs.

“We’re getting better at understanding the ‘pre-game show’ before a big rupture,” said Dr. Houston. “If we see a series of slow-slip events accelerating or changing character, it might raise our concern and prompt closer monitoring of a region. That could mean giving people and emergency services a heads-up, even if it’s only hours or minutes.”

In some regions of the world, such as Japan and Mexico, early warning systems can send alerts after an initial tremor is detected, giving people seconds to prepare before the strongest shaking arrives. These alerts can prompt trains to slow down, factories to shut off sensitive machinery, and individuals to take cover. Better detection of subtle, precursor signals might enhance the lead time or reliability of these warnings, ultimately saving lives and reducing damage.

**Broader Implications for Earth Science**  
While the hunt for Earth’s biggest quakes grabs the headlines, the AI revolution in seismology has broader implications. A bale of hay might look traditional enough, but on a ranch near Camarillo, California, a few Angus steers have been munching something extra in their daily feed: dried seaweed pellets. The unlikely ingredient isn’t a culinary stunt; it’s part of a serious effort to clean up the beef industry’s image—literally. According to a new study led by researchers at the University of California, Davis, adding small amounts of a certain red seaweed to grazing cattle’s diet cut their methane emissions by nearly 40 percent.

For years, scientists have been trying to find ways to reduce livestock-generated methane, a potent greenhouse gas that traps far more heat per unit than carbon dioxide. Although methane doesn’t linger as long in the atmosphere, it packs an outsized punch in the short term, and cattle are notorious for producing it in their rumen as they digest feed. Many proposed fixes have fallen flat, but feeding seaweed—specifically Asparagopsis taxiformis—appears to tamp down certain microbes in a cow’s gut, thus lowering methane belches without harming the animal’s appetite or growth.

“These results surprised us because we tested the additive in a realistic grazing setting, not just in feedlots,” says Ermias Kebreab, an animal scientist at UC Davis and one of the study’s authors. “We had good indications from controlled trials, but we didn’t know how well it would work when cattle roamed on pastureland.” Previous experiments in confined environments showed even larger methane reductions, sometimes more than 50 or 60 percent. Grazing conditions present a tougher challenge, since cows wander and forage at will. Yet the new field trial still recorded an impressive drop in emissions—roughly 30 to 40 percent—over several months.

To apply the treatment, technicians ground the seaweed into powder and compressed it into pellets that could be easily mixed with molasses and other supplements. The cows didn’t seem to mind the taste. In fact, the animals gained weight at rates similar to their herdmates that didn’t eat seaweed, suggesting no loss of feed efficiency. “We were particularly encouraged that animal health and productivity remained steady,” says Breanna Roque, a ruminant nutrition researcher at UC Davis who helped conduct the feeding trials. “We didn’t want a situation where we fixed one problem but caused another, like reduced growth or lower-quality meat.”

Ranchers who followed the study closely say it’s a welcome development, though they remain cautious about scaling it up. Demand for beef is as strong as ever, and producers are under pressure to shrink their environmental footprint. “We’re always told to cut back greenhouse gases, but it’s tough to do without concrete solutions,” says Austin Ramirez, who manages a family-run ranch in the Central Valley. “If seaweed pellets give us a practical tool, that’s worth exploring. Of course, we’ll have to see if the supply chain can handle it and what it costs.”

Cost is no small matter. While researchers didn’t release detailed pricing, growing and harvesting enough Asparagopsis on a commercial scale could prove a bottleneck. The red seaweed thrives in warm, tropical waters, and most of the current supply comes from pilot farms experimenting with cultivation. Still, a handful of companies have sprung up recently, betting that ranchers—and, indirectly, consumers—will pay a slight premium for more climate-friendly beef.

The environmental benefits could be significant. Methane from livestock is a major contributor to agricultural emissions, and curbing it would help countries meet their climate goals. Although cutting methane alone can’t solve global warming, it can buy time, experts argue. “Reducing livestock methane offers a relatively quick win,” says Frank Mitloehner, an air quality specialist at UC Davis who was not involved in this particular study but has researched greenhouse gases for decades. “If we can cut that emission source even by a modest percentage, the climate math gets a little easier in the near term.”

There are questions beyond economics and supply. For instance, how will consumers feel about cows eating seaweed? Surveys suggest that many people wouldn’t mind, as long as it doesn’t alter the flavor or safety of the beef. Preliminary taste tests show no detectable differences, and the FDA has taken a generally positive stance toward such feed additives, though more research might be required before any official green light. That said, the ranching industry can be slow to adopt new methods. Some producers wonder if dried seaweed pellets will be practical in remote pastures or if weather conditions might pose storage challenges.

The study’s authors acknowledge these hurdles. “It’s early days,” Roque says. “We’re encouraged by the data, but we know wide adoption means working out logistics and showing ranchers that it’s worth their while.” Additional long-term trials are planned to monitor animal health, productivity, and the subtle complexities of managing seaweed diets at scale.

For now, the findings show that a modest sprinkle of seaweed can shift the environmental balance in the cattle industry’s favor. The scientists behind the research stress that it won’t solve climate change on its own, but the next time you see cattle grazing quietly on rolling hills, it’s possible a few are sampling seaweed-laced pellets—an underappreciated twist in the quest to reduce agriculture’s carbon hoofprint.

The literal answer to your question 'what determines the price of an ETF' is 'the market'; it is whatever price a buyer is willing to pay and a seller is willing to accept. But if the market price of an ETF share deviates significantly from its NAV, the per-share market value of the securities in its portfolio, then an Authorized Participant can make an arbitrage profit by a transaction (creation or redemption) that pushes the market price toward NAV. Thus as long as the markets are operating and the APs don't vanish in a puff of smoke we can expect price will track NAV. That reduces your question to: why does NAV = market value of the holdings underlying a bond ETF share decrease when the market interest rate rises?  Let's consider an example. I'll use US Treasuries because they have very active markets, are treated as risk-free (although that can be debated), and excluding special cases like TIPS and strips are almost perfectly fungible. And I use round numbers for convenience. Let's assume the current market interest rate is 2% and 'Spindoctor 10-year Treasury Fund' opens for business with $100m invested (via APs) in 10-year T-notes with 2% coupon at par and 1m shares issued that are worth $100 each. Now assume the interest rate goes up to 3% (this is an example NOT A PREDICTION); no one wants to pay par for a 2% bond when they can get 3% elsewhere, so its value goes down to about 0.9 of par (not exactly due to the way the arithmetic works but close enough) and Spindoctor shares similarly slide to $90. At this price an investor gets slightly over 2% (coupon*face/basis) plus approximately 1% amortized capital gain (slightly less due to time value) per year so it's competitive with a 3% coupon at par.  As you say new bonds are available that pay 3%. But our fund doesn't hold them; we hold old bonds with a face value of $100m but a market value of only $90m. If we sell those bonds now and buy 3% bonds to (try to) replace them, we only get $90m par value of 3% bonds, so now our fund is paying a competitive 3% but NAV is still only $90.  At the other extreme, say we hold the 2% bonds to maturity, paying out only 2% interest but letting our NAV increase as the remaining term (duration) and thus discount of the bonds decreases -- assuming the market interest rate doesn't change again, which for 10 years is probably unrealistic (ignoring 2009-2016!). At the end of 10 years the 2% bonds are redeemed at par and our NAV is back to $100 -- but from the investor's point of view they've forgone $10 in interest they could have received from an alternative investment over those 10 years, which is effectively an additional investment, so the original share price of $90 was correct.

I'll mention Apple quickly as a special case that has managed to charge a premium margin for a mass-market product.  Few companies can achieve this. As with all investment analysis, you need to have a very clear understanding of the industry (i.e. what is "normal" for debt/equity/gearing/margin/cash-on-hand) as well as of the barriers-to-entry which competitors face. A higher-than-normal margin may swiftly be undermined by competitors (Apple aside).  Any company offering perpetual above-the-odds returns may just be a Ponzi scheme (Bernie Maddof, etc.).  More important than high-margins or high-profits over some short-term track is consistency of approach, an ability to whether adverse cyclical events, and deep investment in continuity (i.e. the entire company doesn't come to a grinding halt when a crucial staff-member retires).

Mortgage rates are influenced by a variety of economic, political, and other factors. Some of the key factors that can influence mortgage rates include:Market conditions: Mortgage rates are influenced by market conditions, including the overall demand for mortgages, the supply of funds available to lend, and the level of competition among lenders.Inflation: Inflation can have an impact on mortgage rates, as lenders may be more likely to increase rates in order to compensate for the potential for rising prices over time.Economic growth: Strong economic growth can lead to higher demand for mortgages, which can in turn lead to higher mortgage rates. Conversely, slow economic growth may lead to lower mortgage rates.Central bank policy: Central banks, such as the Federal Reserve in the United States, can influence mortgage rates through their monetary policy decisions. For example, if the central bank raises interest rates, mortgage rates may also rise.Political uncertainty: Political uncertainty, such as the possibility of trade wars or changes in government policies, can also influence mortgage rates.Credit availability: The availability of credit can also impact mortgage rates. If credit is readily available, lenders may be more willing to offer lower rates in order to attract borrowers.It's important to note that these factors can interact with one another and that mortgage rates can be influenced by a variety of other factors as well. It's also worth noting that mortgage rates can vary widely depending on the lender, the borrower's credit score and other factors, and may not necessarily move in the same direction as broader market interest rates.

There are several factors that can influence the value of a company, and therefore the value of its stock options. Some of the key factors to consider when trying to approximate the value of a company include:Financial performance: Companies with strong financial performance, such as high revenue, profitability, and growth, are generally more valuable than those with weak financial performance.Market demand: Companies that operate in high-demand markets or that have a unique product or service offering may be more valuable than those operating in less competitive markets.Industry trends: Companies that are well-positioned to take advantage of current and future industry trends are generally more valuable than those that are not.Management team: Companies with strong leadership and a track record of success are generally more valuable than those with weak management.Risk profile: Companies with a lower risk profile are generally more valuable than those with a higher risk profile.To estimate the value of a company, you can use financial metrics such as price-to-earnings ratio (P/E ratio), price-to-sales ratio (P/S ratio), and price-to-book ratio (P/B ratio). You can also use valuation techniques such as discounted cash flow (DCF) analysis and comparable company analysis. It's important to note that there is no one-size-fits-all approach to valuing a company, and the value of a company can vary significantly depending on the method used.

When the temperatures drop and a chill settles in the air, few things comfort as quickly or deliciously as a steaming mug of hot chocolate. But as you wrap your hands around that warm cup, have you ever paused to wonder where this decadent drink originated?

“Chocolate beverages have a rich and ancient heritage,” says Dr. Carla Martin, a chocolate historian at Harvard University. Long before marshmallows were bobbing in sweet milky cocoa, chocolate was consumed by Mesoamerican civilizations. The Mayans and Aztecs of Central America drank a bitter, frothy concoction made from ground cacao beans mixed with water and spices like chili and vanilla. It was a far cry from the sugary treat we know today.

For these early chocolate drinkers, cacao beans weren’t merely a source of pleasure—they were valuable currency and held a sacred place in religious ceremonies. “Chocolate was considered a gift from the gods,” explains Dr. Martin, “and the drinks prepared from it were often consumed by nobility and warriors, believed to provide strength and vitality.”

It wasn’t until European explorers arrived in the Americas that chocolate would shift toward sweetness. When Spanish conquistadors returned home in the 16th century carrying cacao beans and chocolate-making knowledge, Europeans experimented by adding sugar, which had become more readily available. With this one adjustment, the bitter chocolate beverage evolved into a sweet indulgence that quickly spread throughout Europe’s upper classes.

By the 17th and 18th centuries, hot chocolate was a beloved luxury. In France, King Louis XIV’s court savored chocolate drinks at decadent gatherings. Across the English Channel, London’s chocolate houses—like early coffee shops—became fashionable meeting spots where people sipped rich hot cocoa and debated the issues of the day. “Europeans not only embraced chocolate,” says Sarah Mayfield, a food anthropologist in London, “they elevated it. It became associated with sophistication, conversation, and social status.”

As chocolate plantations expanded and production methods improved, prices began to drop, making hot chocolate more accessible. The Industrial Revolution further democratized chocolate, allowing it to be mass-produced and sold to the middle class. By the 19th century, drinking chocolate had crossed the Atlantic again, this time to the United States, where it continued to evolve. Americans refined recipes, sometimes using milk instead of water, yielding the creamy, comforting beverage we love today.

The modern version of hot chocolate most of us enjoy—often made with cocoa powder, sugar, and milk—would probably surprise an ancient Mayan. “It’s sweeter, smoother, and less spicy than the original,” Mayfield notes. “But the essence remains: it’s a comforting drink that warms both body and spirit.”

Today, hot chocolate is experiencing a renaissance. Artisan chocolatiers craft luxurious cocoa blends, and cafés offer gourmet hot chocolate flights featuring unique flavors from around the world. In wintertime, it remains a cherished treat for families, who top it with whipped cream or marshmallows and sip it by a crackling fire.

In many ways, hot chocolate’s journey mirrors our human story—adaptation, exchange of ideas, and the blending of old and new traditions. “With each sip,” says Dr. Martin, “you’re tasting centuries of history, cultural exchange, and innovation.” It’s a delicious reminder that sometimes the simplest pleasures carry the deepest roots.

Rest and elevate the affected ankle: It's important to give your ankle time to heal, so try to avoid putting weight on it as much as possible. When you're sitting or lying down, elevate your ankle on a pillow to help reduce swelling.

Ice the affected area: Applying an ice pack to your ankle for 15-20 minutes every few hours can help reduce swelling and numb the pain.

Compress the affected area: Wrapping your ankle with a compression bandage or using an ankle support can help reduce swelling and provide support to the area.

Take over-the-counter pain medication: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) like ibuprofen or naproxen can help reduce swelling and alleviate pain.

Stretch and strengthen your ankle: Gentle stretches and exercises can help improve flexibility and strength in your ankle, which can help prevent future injuries.

If your ankle pain persists or becomes more severe, you should consider seeking medical attention. It's also a good idea to see a doctor if you have any concerns about your back pain.

It is possible that the pain you are experiencing while urinating and during intercourse could be due to a kidney stone or a urinary tract infection (UTI). However, it is also possible that the pain could be due to something else entirely. It is important to speak with a healthcare provider to determine the cause of the pain and receive proper treatment.

Kidney stones are hard masses made of crystals that form in the kidneys and can cause pain when they move through the urinary tract. The pain associated with kidney stones is typically described as a sharp, cramping pain in the lower back, side, or groin area. It is often accompanied by nausea, vomiting, and blood in the urine.

UTIs are infections of the urinary system, which includes the kidneys, bladder, ureters, and urethra. UTIs can cause symptoms such as pain or burning while urinating, frequent urges to urinate, cloudy or bloody urine, and lower abdominal pain. UTIs can also cause discomfort during intercourse.

It is important to see a healthcare provider for a proper diagnosis and treatment. In the meantime, you can try drinking plenty of water to help flush out your urinary system and relieve some of the pain.

Markets "factor in" a future event by incorporating expectations about the event into asset prices. This can happen through a variety of channels, such as changes in demand for a particular asset, changes in the supply of an asset, or changes in the risk associated with holding an asset.For example, if investors expect that a company will announce strong earnings in the future, they may be more likely to buy the company's stock, which would drive up the price. On the other hand, if investors expect that a company will announce weak earnings, they may be more likely to sell the company's stock, which would drive down the price.In general, financial markets are constantly incorporating new information about the future, and this information is reflected in the prices of assets. When a major event occurs, such as a change in interest rates or the release of economic data, it can have a significant impact on asset prices, as investors and traders adjust their expectations about the future in light of the new information.

Diversification is the only real free lunch in finance (reduction in risk without any reduction in expected returns), so clearly every good answer to your question will be "yes."  Diversification is good."  Let's talk about many details your question solicits. Many funds are already pretty diversified.  If you buy a mutual fund, you are generally already getting a large portion of the gains from diversification.  There is a very large difference between the unnecessary risk in your portfolio if you only hold a couple of stocks and if you hold a mutual fund.  Should you be diversified across mutual funds as well?  It depends on what your funds are.  Many funds, such as target-date funds, are intended to be your sole investment.  If you have funds covering every major asset class, then there may not be any additional benefit to buying other funds. You probably could not have picked your "favorite fund" early on.  As humans, we have cognitive biases that make us think we knew things early on that we did not.  I'm sure at some point at the very beginning you had a positive feeling toward that fund.  Today you regret not acting on it and putting all your money there.  But the number of such feelings is very large and if you acted on all those, you would do a lot of crazy and harmful things.  You didn't know early on which fund would do well.  You could just as well have had a good feeling about a fund that subsequently did much worse than your diversified portfolio did. The advice you have had about your portfolio probably isn't based on sound finance theory.  You say you have always kept your investments in line with your age.  This implies that you believe the guidelines given you by your broker or financial advisor are based in finance theory.  Generally speaking, they are not.  They are rules of thumb that seemed good to someone but are not rigorously proven either in theory or empirics.  For example the notion that you should slowly shift your investments from speculative to conservative as you age is not based on sound finance theory.  It just seems good to the people who give advice on such things.  Nothing particularly wrong with it, I guess, but it's not remotely on par with the general concept of being well-diversified.  The latter is extremely well established and verified, both in theory and in practice.  Don't confuse the concept of diversification with the specific advice you have received from your advisor. A fund averaging very good returns is not an anomaly--at least going forward it will not be.  There are many thousand funds and a large distribution in their historical performance.  Just by random chance, some funds will have a truly outstanding track record.  Perhaps the manager really was skilled.  However, very careful empirical testing has shown the following: (1) You, me, and people whose profession it is to select outperforming mutual funds are unable to reliably detect which ones will outperform, except in hindsight  (2) A fund that has outperformed, even over a long horizon, is not more likely to outperform in the future. No one is stopping you from putting all your money in that fund. Depending on its investment objective, you may even have decent diversification if you do so.  However, please be aware that if you move your money based on historical outperformance, you will be acting on the same cognitive bias that makes gamblers believe they are on a "hot streak" and "can't lose."  They can, and so can you. ======== Edit to answer a more specific line of questions =========== One of your questions is whether it makes sense to buy a number of mutual funds as part of your diversification strategy.  This is a slightly more subtle question and I will indicate where there is uncertainty in my answer.   Diversifying across asset classes.  Most of the gains from diversification are available in a single fund.  There is a lot of idiosyncratic risk in one or two stocks and much less in a collection of hundreds of stocks, which is what any mutual fund will hold.  Still,you will probably want at least a couple of funds in your portfolio.  I will list them from most important to least and I will assume the bulk of your portfolio is in a total US equity fund (or S&P500-style fund) so that you are almost completely diversified already. Risky Bonds.  These are corporate, municipal, sovereign debt, and long-term treasury debt funds. There is almost certainly a good deal to be gained by having a portion of your portfolio in bonds, and normally a total market fund will not include bond exposure.  Bonds fund returns are closely related to interest rate and inflation changes.  They are also exposed to some market risk but it's more efficient to get that from equity.  The bond market is very large, so if you did market weights you would have more in bonds than in equity.  Normally people do not do this, though.  Instead you can get the exposure to interest rates by holding a lesser amount in longer-term bonds, rather than more in shorter-term bonds.  I don't believe in shifting your weights toward nor away from this type of bond (as opposed to equity) as you age so if you are getting that advice, know that it is not well-founded in theory.  Whatever your relative weight in risky bonds when you are young is should also be your weight when you are older. International. There are probably some gains from having some exposure to international markets, although these have decreased over time as economies have become more integrated.  If we followed market weights, you would actually put half your equity weight in an international fund.  Because international funds are taxed differently (gains are always taxed at the short-term capital gains rate) and because they have higher management fees, most people make only a small investment to international funds, if any at all. Emerging markets  International funds often ignore emerging markets in order to maintain liquidity and low fees.  You can get some exposure to these markets through emerging markets funds.  However, the value of public equity in emerging markets is small when compared with that of developed markets, so according to finance theory, your investment in them should be small as well.  That's a theoretical, not an empirical result. Emerging market funds charge high fees as well, so this one is kind of up to your taste.  I can't say whether it will work out in the future. Real estate.  You may want to get exposure to real estate by buying a real-estate fund (REIT).  Though, if you own a house you are already exposed to the real estate market, perhaps more than you want to be.  REITs often invest in commercial real estate, which is a little different from the residential market. Small Cap.  Although total market funds invest in all capitalization levels, the market is so skewed toward large firms that many total market funds don't have any significant small cap exposure.  It's common for individuals to hold a small cap fund to compensate for this, but it's not actually required by investment theory.  In principle, the most diversified portfolio should be market-cap weighted, so small cap should have negligible weight in your portfolio.  Many people hold small cap because historically it has outperformed large cap firms of equal risk, but this trend is uncertain.  Many researchers feel that the small cap "premium" may have been a short-term artifact in the data.  Given these facts and the fact that small-cap funds charge higher fees, it may make sense to pass on this asset class.  Depends on your opinion and beliefs. Value (or Growth) Funds.  Half the market can be classed as "value", while the other half is "growth."  Your total market fund should have equal representation in both so there is no diversification reason to buy a special value or growth fund.  Historically, value funds have outperformed over long horizons and many researchers think this will continue, but it's not exactly mandated by the theory.  If you choose to skew your portfolio by buying one of these, it should be a value fund. Sector funds.  There is, in general, no diversification reason to buy funds that invest in a particular sector.  If you are trying to hedge your income (like trying to avoid investing in the tech sector because you work in that sector) or your costs (buying energy because you buy use a disproportionate amount of energy) I could imagine you buying one of these funds. Risk-free bonds.  Funds specializing in short-term treasuries or short-term high-quality bonds of other types are basically a substitute for a savings account, CD, money market fund, or other cash equivalent.  Use as appropriate but there is little diversification here per se. In short, there is some value in diversifying across asset classes, and it is open to opinion how much you should do.  Less well-justified is diversifying across managers within the same asset class.  There's very little if any advantage to doing that.

Parents have always blamed their teens’ misbehavior on their kids’ friends: they may say their kids “fell into bad company” or “got in with the wrong crowd.” To combat what they see as pernicious influences, parents have responded with strategies that range from criticizing the wayward companions to forbidding any contact altogether. This type of response by parents has been documented from the Netherlands to China. 

In fact, the question remains as to whether placing these supposed bad influences off-limits actually helps children. “Not a bit” is the answer, according to child psychology researchers. In fact, this type of response actually backfires. As researchers have found in several studies, parents’ disapproval or restrictions on hanging out with a supposed bad actor actually makes behavior problems worse—and the experts are not exactly sure why that is. “People have seen this; they scratch their heads and say they’re not sure what to make of it,” says Florida Atlantic University psychologist Brett Laursen. 

Previous research has provided a partial explanation that fits with most parents’ experience. As kids begin to forge identities separate from their parents, they resist parental direction and control. As the father characters in the musical The Fantasticks sing, “You can be sure the devil’s to pay/The minute that you say no.” One study entitled “Forbidden Friends as Forbidden Fruit,” from researchers at Utrecht University in the Netherlands, demonstrated this truism with a sample of Dutch boys aged about 13. The researchers found that when their parents forbade them to associate with friends who were got in trouble, the boys sought out and clung to these off-limits friends. The result? Their own troublemaking, defined as behaviors including vandalism, theft and arson, increased. 

Such rebellious behavior provides only a piece of the answer. These interactions are actually a complex mix of motivations. Laursen, with his co-author Goda Kaniušonytė, sets out a broader explanation in a new study. Researchers questioned almost 600 Lithuanian boys and girls aged 9 to 14 at the beginning, middle and end of a school year. At each point, the students answered a range of questions on tablets about their emotions, their behavior (from shoplifting to breaking windows), their relationship with their mother, and their mother’s feelings about the friends they had and the ones their mom wished they had—the good students, for example. 

An important dimension was included that had not been considered in previous research. The researchers measured maternal disapproval at each point in time. They also asked the children to list classmates that they liked, disliked or found disruptive. 

A clear pattern emerged. Whenever a child had behavior problems—and their mother disapproved of their friends —these peers, in turn, then disliked the child and the kid’s behavior got worse. That behavior problems are linked to rejection makes sense, Laursen says. “The mystery is, why did mom’s intervention lead to more problems? And it’s because the classmates hate it. Kids hate parents intervening in peer relationships.” He adds that rejected kids tend to hang out with other excluded kids who themselves are likely to have behavior problems. 

The idea that parental interference in peer friendships can make a child seem “uncool” to peers and set them off on a disruptive trajectory is a really new insight, says Northern Illinois University developmental psychologist Nina Mounts. It fits with research showing that prohibitions are probably not a good strategy for parents, she says. “Consulting with kids, on the other hand, leads to more prosocial behavior, more empathy and better social skills.” 

Tensions around finding their place can make it difficult to navigate the perils of being a teenager. “Adolescence is a very anxious time,” says Vanessa Bradden, a family therapist based in Chicago. “Kids are trying to figure out who their peers are.” Although parents may be tempted to express dislike for certain friendships, she says it is probably better to hold back judgment and express understanding for your child’s situation, including how urgently they need to fit in with their peers. You might suggest, “I know kids are vaping and drinking, but I’m most concerned with what you’re doing and how you can be safe.” If you find out your child has been doing something dangerous with friends, you can express how serious it is and implement an appropriate punishment—maybe to stay home after school for two weeks with no video games. But saying they can no longer be friends with someone should not be the punishment, she advises. 

Boston Children’s Hospital clinical psychologist Erica Lee counsels parents to take a deep breath, try to stay calm and to understand what their child actually did and why. You may have only part of the story, she says. “It’s important to say to your kids, I want to understand what happened from your perspective.” You can ask them why certain friends are so attractive to them even though they enable behavior that results in bad consequences. Thus only reporting a negative item to Experian will mean that TransUnion and Equifax scores for the same person will be higher.

In recent years, the beverage industry has witnessed a significant shift as more consumers gravitate towards non-alcoholic (NA) options. Whether it's beer, wine, or spirits, the sales of these alcohol-free alternatives are soaring. But what exactly are these beverages, and how do they stack up in terms of health benefits? The Rise of Non-Alcoholic Beverages The surge in popularity of non-alcoholic beverages can be attributed to several factors. A growing number of people are adopting healthier lifestyles, and many are choosing to reduce or eliminate alcohol consumption altogether. According to a report by Nielsen, sales of non-alcoholic beer, wine, and spirits increased by over 30% in the past year alone. This trend is not just limited to those abstaining from alcohol; even regular drinkers are incorporating NA options into their routines. "People are becoming more health-conscious and are looking for ways to enjoy social occasions without the negative effects of alcohol," says Dr. Emily Roberts, a nutritionist and wellness expert. "Non-alcoholic beverages offer a way to participate in social drinking without the hangover or health risks associated with alcohol." What’s in Non-Alcoholic Beverages? Non-alcoholic beverages are crafted to mimic the taste and experience of their alcoholic counterparts, but with little to no alcohol content. By definition, non-alcoholic beers and wines contain less than 0.5% alcohol by volume (ABV). The process of making these beverages often involves removing alcohol from the finished product or halting fermentation before alcohol is produced. For non-alcoholic spirits, the process can be more complex. Many brands use a combination of botanicals, herbs, and spices to replicate the flavors of traditional spirits. "The goal is to create a sensory experience similar to that of drinking alcohol," explains Mark Thompson, a beverage industry analyst. "It's about capturing the essence of the drink without the alcohol." Are Non-Alcoholic Beverages Healthy? When it comes to health, non-alcoholic beverages offer several advantages over their alcoholic counterparts. For starters, they eliminate the risks associated with alcohol consumption, such as liver damage, addiction, and impaired judgment. Additionally, many NA options are lower in calories, making them a suitable choice for those watching their weight. However, it's important to note that not all non-alcoholic beverages are created equal. Some may contain added sugars or artificial ingredients to enhance flavor. "Consumers should be mindful of the ingredients list," advises Dr. Roberts. "Opt for brands that use natural ingredients and minimal additives." Hydration is another factor to consider. While non-alcoholic beverages can be a refreshing alternative, they should not replace water as the primary source of hydration. "It's easy to forget that these drinks, although non-alcoholic, are not a substitute for water," says Dr. Roberts. "Staying hydrated is crucial for overall health." The Social Aspect Beyond health, non-alcoholic beverages play a significant role in social settings. They provide an inclusive option for those who choose not to drink alcohol, whether for health, religious, or personal reasons. "Having a non-alcoholic option at social gatherings can make a big difference," says Sarah Johnson, founder of a popular sober-curious community. "It allows everyone to feel included and part of the celebration." The rise of the "sober curious" movement has also contributed to the popularity of NA beverages. This movement encourages individuals to explore their relationship with alcohol and consider reducing their intake. "It's about being mindful of how alcohol affects your life and making conscious choices," explains Johnson. The Future of Non-Alcoholic Beverages As the demand for non-alcoholic beverages continues to grow, the industry is responding with innovation and variety. From craft breweries to established wine producers, more brands are entering the NA market, offering consumers a wider range of options. "The future looks bright for non-alcoholic beverages," says Thompson. "We're seeing more creativity and quality in the products being offered, which is exciting for consumers." In conclusion, non-alcoholic beverages are more than just a trend; they represent a shift in how people approach drinking. With their health benefits, social inclusivity, and expanding variety, NA options are here to stay. Whether you're looking to cut back on alcohol or simply want to try something new, non-alcoholic beverages offer a refreshing alternative that caters to a diverse range of preferences and lifestyles.

You say you have 90% in stocks. I'll assume that you have the other 10% in bonds. For the sake of simplicity, I'll assume that your investments in stocks are in nice, passive indexed mutual funds and ETFs, rather than in individual stocks. A 90% allocation in stocks is considered aggressive. The problem is that if the stock market crashes, you may lose 40% or more of your investment in a single year. As you point out, you are investing for the long term. That's great, it means you can rest easy if the stock market crashes, safe in the hope that you have many years for it to recover. So long as you have the emotional willpower to stick with it. Would you be better off with a 100% allocation in stocks? You'd think so, wouldn't you. After all, the stock market as a whole gives better expected returns than the bond market. But keep in mind, the stock market and the bond market are (somewhat) negatively correlated. That means when the stock market goes down, the bond market often goes up, and vice versa. Investing some of your money in bonds will slightly reduce your expected return but will also reduce your standard deviation and your maximum annual loss. Canadian Couch Potato has an interesting write-up on how to estimate stock and bond returns. It's based on your stocks being invested equally in the Canadian, U.S., and international markets. As you live in the U.S., that likely doesn't directly apply to you; you probably ignore the Canadian stock market, but your returns will be fairly similar. I've reproduced part of that table here: As you can see, your expected return is highest with a 100% allocation in stocks. With a 20 year window, you likely can recover from any crash. If you have the stomach for it, it's the allocation with the highest expected return. Once you get closer to retirement, though, you have less time to wait for the stock market to recover. If you still have 90% or 100% of your investment in stocks and the market crashes by 44%, it might well take you more than 6 years to recover. Canadian Couch Potato has another article, Does a 60/40 Portfolio Still Make Sense? A 60/40 portfolio is a fairly common split for regular investors. Typically considered not too aggressive, not too conservative. The article references an AP article that suggests, in the current financial climate, 60/40 isn't enough. Even they aren't recommending a 90/10 or a 100/0 split, though. Personally, I think 60/40 is too conservative. However, I don't have the stomach for a 100/0 split or even a 90/10 split. Okay, to get back to your question. So long as your time horizon is far enough out, the expected return is highest with a 100% allocation in stocks. Be sure that you can tolerate the risk, though. A 30% or 40% hit to your investments is enough to make anyone jittery. Investing a portion of your money in bonds slightly lowers your expected return but can measurably reduce your risk. As you get closer to retirement and your time horizon narrows, you have less time to recover from a stock market crash and do need to be more conservative. 6 years is probably too short to keep all your money in stocks. Is your stated approach reasonable? Well, only you can answer that. :)

In 1954, a gigantic beast surfaced from the Pacific Ocean, causing widespread devastation. This creature was Godzilla, a manifestation of the global dread and unease following the era of nuclear conflict. Seven decades on, Godzilla continues to be a cultural icon, serving not only as a representation of cinematic grandeur but also as a powerful reminder of the human influence on the planet.

Ishirō Honda's original "Godzilla" movie premiered in Japan during a period when the memories of Hiroshima and Nagasaki remained vivid. The storyline of the film was directly influenced by the atomic bombings and the later hydrogen bomb experiments in the Pacific. Godzilla, brought to life and strengthened by nuclear radiation, symbolized the catastrophic potential of misused human technology. Raymond Burr, who appeared in the American adaptation of the film, once said, "Godzilla serves as a cautionary tale, highlighting the dangers we might unleash if we aren't vigilant."

Throughout the years, Godzilla has transformed, featuring in various movies that mirror the environmental and social issues of their respective eras. Yoshimitsu Banno, who directed the 1971 movie "Godzilla vs. Hedorah," utilized the creature to highlight the escalating problem of pollution. In this movie, Godzilla fights a monster created by industrial pollution, emphasizing the risks of ignoring environmental issues. Banno expressed, "My aim was to demonstrate that pollution is a monster of our own making, and it is our responsibility to put an end to it."

Godzilla's environmental theme aligns with the efforts of environmentalists such as Rachel Carson, whose influential 1962 book "Silent Spring" cautioned against the excessive use of pesticides and their harmful effects on ecosystems. Similar to Godzilla, Carson's work acted as an alarm, prompting society to reevaluate its connection with the natural world. "We are at a crossroads," Carson noted, "One path is the familiar, effortless route, a fast-moving highway, but it ultimately leads to catastrophe."

In a similar vein, Japanese author Michiko Ishimure, recognized for her advocacy against mercury poisoning in Minamata, Japan, shared these views. Her work underscored the harmful impact of industrial pollution on both communities and ecosystems. Ishimure's works, akin to the Godzilla movies, highlighted the link between human behavior and the well-being of the environment. "We need to heed the Earth's warnings," Ishimure insisted, "as they reflect the fate that awaits us."

Marking Godzilla's 70th anniversary, it's important to consider the insights this legendary creature has provided. Today's environmental issues, such as climate change, loss of biodiversity, and pollution, demand immediate attention more than ever before. The lasting impact of Godzilla highlights the effectiveness of storytelling in increasing awareness and motivating change.

Lately, the Godzilla series has kept tackling modern-day challenges. The 2019 movie "Godzilla: King of the Monsters" delved into the ideas of maintaining ecological balance and the effects of human disruption on nature. Director Michael Dougherty stated, "Godzilla represents a natural power, reminding us that we are not in charge. We need to find a way to live in harmony with nature rather than trying to control it.

The theme of living in harmony is especially pertinent as we face the challenges posed by climate change. Researchers caution that increasing temperatures, thawing ice caps, and severe weather phenomena indicate a planet under duress. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) has consistently urged for immediate measures to cut carbon emissions and shift towards renewable energy solutions. "The chance to act is diminishing," cautions Dr. Jane Goodall, a famous primatologist and environmental advocate. "It is imperative that we take immediate steps to safeguard our planet for those who will come after us."

The tale of Godzilla serves as a warning that failing to act can lead to disastrous outcomes. The creature's destructive actions symbolize the possible ruin caused by uncontrolled environmental harm. However, Godzilla also symbolizes hope—the chance for redemption and renewal if humanity opts for an alternative course.

Looking ahead, it's crucial to pay attention to the lessons within Godzilla's story. The creature's roar resonates as a pressing appeal for responsible environmental care and sustainable practices. Adopting these principles will help secure a healthier world for both current and future generations.

Ultimately, Godzilla's 70th anniversary is not merely a tribute to a film legend; it serves as a rallying cry for action. The lasting influence of the creature prompts us to consider our connection with the planet and to acknowledge the consequences of our behavior. Confronting the environmental issues of the 21st century, we should recall Godzilla's lessons and work towards a future where humanity and nature live in balance.

Market price is just the bid or offer price of the last sell or buy order in the market. The price that you actually receive or pay will be the price that the person buying the stock off you or selling it to you will accept. If there are no other participants in the market to make up the other side of your order (i.e. to buy off you if you are selling or to sell to you if you are buying) the exchange pays large banks to be "market makers"; they fulfil your order using stocks that they don't want to either buy or sell just so that you get your order filled. When you place an order outside of market hours the order is kept on the broker's order books until the market reopens and then, at market opening time there is an opening "auction" at which orders are matched to opposing orders (i.e. each buy order will be matched with a sell) at a price determined by auction. You will not know what price the order was filled at until it has been filled. If you want to guarantee a price you can do so by placing a limit order that says not to pay more than a certain price for any unit of the stock.

Q: I can never figure out how best to time my meals with my workouts. Should I be eating before I exercise or after? We’ve all been there: It’s 6 p.m. and you just got home from work. You want to go for a run, but you’re hungry. Should you eat dinner first and risk an upset stomach? Or should you run first, with potentially less energy to power you through? It’s a question that plagues even the most disciplined exercisers among us. And to make the matter even more complicated, research on the topic is limited, with answers that depend on your unique health and goals. That said, experts agree that there are some general considerations to keep in mind. What to Eat and When Health experts recommend eating both before and after exercise, for different reasons. For most people, having a balanced meal rich in carbohydrates and protein two to four hours before a workout will supply enough energy to last the length of your routine. This also allows ample time for digestion and can help reduce gastrointestinal discomfort like nausea, vomiting or acid reflux, said Dr. Martha Gulati, a cardiologist at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles who specializes in helping her patients make lifestyle changes through diet and exercise. If you have a few hours before you plan to exercise, a pre-workout meal might include a high-quality protein (like salmon, chicken or tofu), a complex carbohydrate (like brown rice, oatmeal or sweet potatoes) and healthy sources of fats (like avocado, eggs or nuts), said Dr. Cecilia Cordova Vallejos, a sports medicine physiatrist at Johns Hopkins Medicine. Having a snack about 30 minutes before your workout will also give you an energy boost — especially if you’re doing moderate or high-intensity exercise for longer than 90 minutes, Dr. Cordova Vallejos said. She recommended a protein bar or even just an energy gel packet because they are easy on the stomach. Dr. Gulati suggested a banana or a piece of your favorite fruit. Once you’re done with your workout, aim to consume protein — ideally 20 to 40 grams within two hours, the International Society of Sports Nutrition recommends — to help support muscle growth and recovery. A can of tuna, a chicken breast or three scrambled eggs with cheese would each fall within that range. Your Meal Planning May Depend on Specific Goals The timing of your meals may also depend on your health or fitness objectives. If you have a condition like diabetes where you must manage your blood sugar levels, the recommendations are a little more nuanced, said Jill Kanaley, a professor of nutrition and exercise physiology at the University of Missouri. Some research suggests that those with Type 2 diabetes may be better off having breakfast before they exercise. In one 2017 study of 64 adults with Type 2 diabetes in India, for instance, researchers found that those who had breakfast before exercising had much better blood sugar control than those who didn’t eat before their workout. For people with Type 1 diabetes, the suggestions may be different, Dr. Kanaley added. Some research suggests, for instance, that fasting before a moderate or high-intensity morning workout can be safe and potentially even preferable for people with Type 1 diabetes, depending on your glucose levels upon waking. Though in general, working out on an empty stomach may come with downsides. In one online survey of about 2,000 endurance athletes published in 2020, participants who said they avoided exercising on an empty stomach said they did so because it didn’t help their training, it hampered their athletic performance and it made them hungrier. If you’d like to reduce soreness and improve muscle growth and repair after your workouts, eating a little more protein — and spreading it throughout the day — might help you achieve that goal, Dr. Cordova Vallejos said. If you have food allergies or other dietary restrictions or medical conditions, consider consulting a physician, sports medicine doctor or sports nutritionist to figure out a plan that meets your needs. The Bottom Line The most important thing you should do is pay attention to how your body feels when you eat (or don’t eat) before exercise. If you have a protein- or fat-rich snack 30 minutes before a morning workout and it upsets your stomach, Dr. Gulati said, try switching to a snack that has a higher carbohydrate concentration. Or if you’re doing a lower intensity workout, like a slow walk or yoga, maybe you don’t need to eat first. Over time, you’ll figure out what your body needs, she added. “There isn’t a perfect science,” Dr. Gulati said. Everyone has different needs, goals, diets and schedules, she added, but if you’re patient, you’ll find a routine that works for you.

The market maker will always compare the highest bid and the lowest ask. A trade will happen if the highest bid is at least as high as the lowest ask. Adding one share (or a million shares) at a higher asking price, here: $210 instead of $200, will not have any effect at all. Nobody will buy the share.  Adding a bid for one share (or a million shares) at a higher bid price will trigger a sale. If you bid $210 for one share, you will pay $210 for one of the shares that were offered at $200. If you have $210 million in cash and add a bid for 1,000,000 AAPL at $210, you will pay $210 for all shares with an ask of $200.00, then $200.01, then $200.02 until you either bought all shares with an ask up to $210, or until you bought a million shares.  With AAPL, you probably bid the price up to $201 with a million shares, so you made lots of people very happy while losing about 10 million dollars. So let's say this is a much smaller company. Until some people think there is something going on and enter higher bids, but then some people will take advantage of this and ask lower than your $210. And there will be more people trying to make cash by selling their shares at a good price than people tricked into bidding over $200, so it is most likely that you lose out. Election Day is fundamental to democracy, as it is when citizens cast their votes and influence the future of their communities and nation. Yet, in the midst of the enthusiasm and responsibility, voters must adhere to an essential guideline to make sure their opinions count: refrain from electioneering at the polling place.

Electioneering involves engaging in actions aimed at swaying voters within a specified range of a polling location. This may involve donning campaign clothing, handing out pamphlets, or talking about candidates and topics. Although it might appear innocuous to show your political views, doing so at the polling place can result in significant repercussions, such as being removed before you have the chance to vote.

Wendy Underhill, who leads Elections and Redistricting at the National Conference of State Legislatures, stresses the need to keep polling locations impartial. "The aim is to establish an environment where voters can choose without any coercion or sway," she clarifies. "Laws against electioneering exist to safeguard the voting process's integrity and guarantee that all voters can cast their ballots freely, without intimidation or pressure."

Every state sets its own distinct regulations on electioneering, detailing the prohibited distance from the polling site for these activities. In numerous states, the standard distance is usually 100 feet from the entrance, though it may differ. Voters should ensure they understand their state's rules before going to vote. Not knowing the law doesn't exempt you, and breaking these regulations might lead to being told to take off any campaign gear or, in certain situations, being refused access to the polling place.

Vice President Kamala Harris, a strong supporter of voting rights, frequently emphasizes the significance of engaging in elections and honoring the electoral process. "She has stated that voting is both a right and a duty." "Everyone needs to contribute to making sure the process remains just and free from improper influence." This involves adhering to the regulations and maintaining the sanctity of the voting environment.

Here are some useful suggestions to help you steer clear of problems on Election Day:

Ensure you don't wear any attire or accessories showing support for a candidate or political party before going to vote. This encompasses items like caps, pins, and shirts. Should you mistakenly wear such items, be ready to conceal or take them off prior to entering the polling station.

2. **Steer Clear of Political Conversations**: Do not engage in talks about candidates, political parties, or ballot issues while in line or within the polling station. Maintain discussions on neutral, non-political subjects.

3. **Honor the Restricted Area**: Stay mindful of the specified area around the polling station where electioneering activities are not allowed. If you're uncertain about the designated area, it's usually marked, but you can also ask a poll worker for assistance.

4. **Inform Yourself**: Prior to Election Day, make an effort to understand the electioneering regulations specific to your state. You can typically find this information on your state's election website or by reaching out to your local election office.

5. **Notify Authorities**: If you observe any electioneering or questionable behavior at your polling location, promptly inform a poll worker or election official. They are equipped to manage these scenarios and maintain the fairness and neutrality of the voting process.

Adhering to these recommendations will support the integrity of the electoral process and guarantee that your vote is counted. Keep in mind that Election Day involves more than simply voting; it's about engaging in a democratic process that honors the rights and voices of every citizen.

Ultimately, although you might feel inclined to share your political opinions on Election Day, doing so at the polling place could risk your opportunity to cast a vote. Wendy Underhill aptly emphasizes that maintaining the sanctity of the polling place is of utmost importance. It is a space where voters ought to feel at liberty to decide without external pressure. By following this guideline, you help uphold a fair and democratic election, guaranteeing that each vote is made in a setting of respect and impartiality.

In short selling, an investor sells a security that they do not own, with the intention of buying it back at a lower price in the future and profiting from the price difference. To be able to sell a security that they do not own, the investor must borrow the security from someone who does own it. This is typically done through a broker, who will locate the security and arrange for it to be borrowed on the investor's behalf.There are several reasons why short selling requires borrowing. First, it allows the investor to sell a security that they do not own, which is necessary in order to profit from a decline in its price. Second, it allows the investor to fulfill their obligation to deliver the security to the buyer when the sale is settled. Finally, it ensures that the investor can buy the security back at a later date, as they are required to return the borrowed security to its owner once they have finished their short position.Overall, short selling requires borrowing because it is a way for investors to profit from falling prices in the market, and borrowing is an essential part of the process.

An ETF (Exchange Traded Fund) is a type of investment fund that holds a collection of assets, such as stocks, bonds, or commodities, and is traded on a stock exchange. In general, an ETF is intended to track the performance of its underlying holdings, so it is expected to perform in a similar way to its holdings. However, there are a few factors that can cause an ETF to perform differently than its holdings:Fees and Expenses: ETFs charge fees to cover the costs of managing the fund, such as administrative expenses and investment management fees. These fees can reduce the overall return of the ETF, which could cause it to underperform its holdings.Tracking Error: ETFs aim to closely track the performance of their underlying holdings, but there can be differences between the ETF's performance and the performance of its holdings due to a variety of factors, such as rebalancing, liquidity, and trading costs. This difference is known as tracking error.Market Factors: ETFs are subject to the same market forces as individual stocks, such as supply and demand, economic conditions, and investor sentiment. These factors can affect the price of the ETF, regardless of the performance of its holdings.In summary, while an ETF is generally expected to track the performance of its underlying holdings, there are a number of factors that can cause it to perform differently.
