Deep-sea exploration has long been largely a privilege of billionaires, fossil fuel companies, and a select few scientists from wealthy nations. This exclusivity has left the vast majority of the deep sea unexplored, its natural wonders understudied and vulnerable to exploitation. In recent years, scientists and conservationists have called for the democratization of the deep sea. They say this extreme region of the planet needs to be accessible to everyone. Now, a group of scientists, conservationists, and explorers has devised a low-cost device that is helping bring that goal closer to reality.

Called the Maka Niu, which means “coconut eye” in Hawaiian, the device was initially created by scientists at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and is now being developed by the nonprofit Ocean Discovery League. Looking like little more than a piece of PVC pipe stuffed with gadgets, the compact, customizable, and relatively inexpensive battery-powered data collector can capture video and measure depth, temperature, and salinity at depths as great as 1,500 meters. That’s about five times deeper than even the most specially trained scuba diver can go and deep enough to reach the ocean’s midnight zone, home to deep-sea animals like the vampire squid and chambered nautilus.

A newer version of the Maka Niu can go even deeper says Katy Croff Bell, the deep-sea explorer, scientist, founder of the Ocean Discovery League, and leader of the MIT team. “We have designs that can go to 6,000 meters, which would enable it to reach 99 percent of the seafloor,” she says.

Bell is a vocal advocate for improving equity in deep-sea science, and she hopes the device will aid in the democratization of the deep by giving people the ability to observe it without being reliant on large corporations and the uber-wealthy.

“Ninety-three percent of the ocean is deep sea,” says Bell, “but the technologies that exist today to explore that massive area are expensive, inefficient, and inequitably distributed around the world.”

Costing around US $700 to build, the Maka Niu is looking to buck that trend. It’s supported by a highly programmable Raspberry Pi computer chip, which means users can easily add additional sensors to meet their research needs. This device could help scientists, both professional and citizen, discover new species and explore never-before-seen habitats. It could also, says Bell, help communities gather the baseline data needed to monitor the impacts of human activities such as seafloor mining, which threatens to disturb sensitive deep-sea ecosystems by stirring up sediment and damaging habitats that take millions of years to develop.

As they began developing the Maka Niu, Bell and the MIT team sent prototypes to more than a dozen scientists, educators, fishers, and Indigenous people from 11 countries, all of whom provided recommendations on how to improve the device to meet their specific needs. Now, a new crop of improved prototypes is in the hands of scientists in Sri Lanka, Seychelles, the Cook Islands, South Africa, Montserrat, and Portugal, and in Hawaiʻi and Louisiana in the United States.

This technology, says Jon Copley, a deep-sea biologist at the University of Southampton in England who was not involved in the Maka Niu’s creation, will “create opportunities for people anywhere around the world to get involved in deep-ocean science like never before.”

“There are loads of places where you could put this in the ocean straight away and find out things you didn’t know,” Copley says. “This is potentially such a powerful tool for connecting local communities with what’s right off their shores.”

Creating such a connection, Copley says, is a great way to improve conservation of the deep sea. “There’s a saying that you can’t manage what you can’t observe,” he says.

Although the Maka Niu is still being developed, Bell hopes this technology will inspire others to create similar devices and put them to use around the world.

“My hope is that systems like this will be in the hands of a much larger community of ocean explorers around the world who are using them for their own research. And I can’t wait to see what they find and learn,” she says.


KNaCK works by measuring the distances of surfaces and nearby objects with a pulsed laser, reports Gizmodo's Passant Rabie. The laser, a frequency modulated continuous wave (FMCW) lidar, can measure millions of points per second. The lidar then creates a map of the surrounding terrain. As a result, it will allow astronauts to scout less-explored regions on the moon. NASA's dynamic technology is like the technology used by smart cars to alert their drivers of potential collisions, reports Loukia Papadopoulos for Interesting Engineering. The laser can pick up details like the landscape's topography, such as deep ravines, caves and mountains, even in complete darkness.

"Basically, the sensor is a surveying tool for both navigation and science mapping, able to create ultra-high-resolution 3-D maps at centimeter-level precision and give them a rich scientific context," tells Michael Zanetti, planetary scientist and project lead of KNaCK, in a statement. "It also will help ensure the safety of astronauts and rover vehicles in a GPS-denied environment such as the Moon, identifying actual distances to far-off landmarks and showing explorers in real time how far they've come and how far is left to go to reach their destination."

As part of the Artemis program, NASA plans to have astronauts return to the moon by 2025. The team is set to land near the lunar south pole because previous evidence suggests that the area may contain subsurface water ice, per Gizmodo. Part of the reason astronauts would need a GPS tracking backpack like KNaCK is because the area on the moon's south pole is shrouded by shadows, making it difficult for space explorers to estimate distances on the moon. KNaCK will also let astronauts estimate the exact amount of oxygen they will need to complete missions while on the moon, Gizmodo reports.

"As human beings, we tend to orient ourselves based on landmarks—a specific building, a grove of trees," Zanetti says in a statement. "Those things don't exist on the moon. KNaCK will continuously enable explorers traversing the surface to determine their movement, direction, and orientation to distant peaks or to their base of operations. They can even mark specific sites where they found some unique mineral or rock formation, so others can easily return for further study."

Next, NASA is working on bringing the backpack's weight and size down. Currently, KNaCK weighs 40 pounds, but the team is envisioning that the tech could be small enough to fit on an astronaut's helmet, per Interesting Engineering.

On the rugged shores of New Zealand’s southeastern coast, the yellow-eyed penguin, or **hoiho**, is facing a dire struggle. The species, known for its distinctive, pale-yellow eyes and shy demeanor, has experienced steep population declines in recent decades due to threats like habitat loss, predators, and disease. Now, a team of dedicated scientists and conservationists is stepping in with extraordinary measures—ranging from hand-feeding “fish smoothies” to administering oral antibiotics—in a last-ditch effort to ensure the survival of one of the world’s rarest penguins.

“We’ve reached a critical turning point,” says Dr. Mel Young, a seabird ecologist at the Department of Conservation in New Zealand. “Without intervention, we risk losing this species entirely.” Once abundant along the country’s coastline, fewer than 3,000 yellow-eyed penguins are believed to remain. Their nesting sites have been disrupted by human development and introduced predators such as stoats and ferrets, while warming oceans have affected the availability of their preferred prey.

Conservationists have adopted a hands-on approach to boost penguin health and help fledglings reach maturity. This often involves rescuing underweight chicks and delivering nutrient-rich “fish smoothies”—a carefully blended mixture of fish fillets and essential supplements—to help them gain strength. “Feeding them directly ensures that they get enough calories and critical nutrients when the natural food supply is uncertain,” explains Dr. Young. “It’s like giving them a jump-start on life.”

In addition to nutritional support, the team has pioneered using oral antibiotics to treat and prevent the spread of respiratory infections that have plagued the population. Administering medicine to wild penguins isn’t easy; it requires gentle restraint and skillful delivery to avoid stressing the birds. “We’re essentially acting as their temporary guardians,” says Rachel Harrington, a wildlife veterinarian involved in the project. “Treating infections promptly prevents further weakening of the population.”

Beyond direct medical care, researchers are also focusing on environmental management. They are restoring native coastal vegetation to shelter the penguins’ nesting areas and installing predator-proof fences to ward off invasive species. “Habitat restoration and predator control go hand in hand with medical intervention,” Harrington notes. “We’re trying to address the root causes of their decline as well as treating immediate health issues.”

This unconventional, labor-intensive approach has already yielded some encouraging results. Over the past few breeding seasons, more chicks have survived to fledge, slowly stabilizing local populations. It’s a delicate balance—wild animals generally fare best without human interference, but the dire circumstances demanded action. “Ideally, we would want these penguins to thrive on their own,” Dr. Young explains. “But at this point, our involvement may be the difference between their survival and extinction.”

In the long run, the hope is that by improving conditions and bolstering penguin health, the species can rebuild robust populations without constant human care. “It’s about buying time,” says Harrington. “By offering a helping hand now, we give these remarkable birds a fighting chance to recover and, one day, stand on their own flippers again.”

This mission, which is a component of NASA's larger initiative to investigate the outer solar system, aims to assess if Europa's ocean could sustain life similar to that on Earth. "The ocean hidden beneath its thick ice layer could potentially harbor conditions suitable for life."

"This mission aims to determine if Europa possesses the essential elements for life to develop."

A key goal of the mission is to evaluate how thick Europa's ice layer is and how deep its ocean extends. Researchers think that the ocean, heated by tidal forces from Jupiter's strong gravitational pull, might interact with the moon's rocky mantle, possibly forming a livable environment. "The interaction between the ocean and the rocky seabed might supply the chemical energy essential for sustaining life," stated Laurie Leshin, a prominent astrobiologist.

The spacecraft will additionally look for water vapor plumes that could be emerging from Europa's surface. If verified, these plumes might provide insight into the ocean's makeup without needing to penetrate the ice. "Identifying and studying these plumes could revolutionize our understanding," remarked Gina DiBraccio, a project scientist involved in the mission. "It would enable us to analyze Europa's ocean indirectly and search for indications of life."

This mission to Europa is a component of a larger initiative to investigate the outer solar system and assess the possibility of life existing beyond our planet. Despite the valuable insights gained from NASA's earlier missions to Jupiter and its moons, Europa continues to be one of the most fascinating subjects of study. "Europa is a realm full of marvels," Mishra commented. "The possibility that it could support life makes it a top exploration target."

The spacecraft will take several years to reach Europa, during which it will conduct multiple flybys to collect data and adjust its course. Upon reaching Europa, the spacecraft will circle the moon and carry out comprehensive surveys, transmitting data back to Earth for scientists to analyze. "This mission exemplifies human curiosity and our drive to investigate the unknown," stated Free. "We are close to finding out if Europa might serve as another habitat for life within our solar system."

As the spacecraft sets off on its mission, both scientists and space enthusiasts are excitedly awaiting the findings it will reveal. "The quest to discover life outside of Earth is among the most significant inquiries we can pursue," stated Leshin. "This mission moves us nearer to finding an answer." The mission, with its ability to unveil the mysteries of Europa's ocean, marks a major advancement in our pursuit to comprehend the universe and our role in it.

Most corporations have a limit on the number of shares that they can issue, which is written into their corporate charter.  They usually sell a number that is fewer than the maximum authorized number so that they have a reserve for secondary offerings, employee incentives, etc. In a scrip dividend, the company is distributing authorized shares that were not previously issued.  This reduces the number of shares that it has to sell in the future to raise capital, so it reduces the assets of the company. In a split, every share (including the authorized shares that haven't been distributed) are divided.  This results in more total shares (which then trade at a price that's roughly proportional to the split), but it does not reduce the assets of the company.

Infarction is most commonly used to refer to a heart attack, but it can also refer to a stroke or the death of tissue in other organs or limbs.

If the blockage is not promptly treated, it can lead to damage or death of the heart muscle tissue in the affected area, known as a myocardial infarction or heart attack.

Today, thanks to her service dog Apollo, she's rediscovering what it means to live without fear.

O'Brien is one of hundreds of veterans who have found relief through K9s For Warriors, a nonprofit organization that pairs trained service dogs with veterans suffering from PTSD, traumatic brain injury, and military sexual trauma.

"Before Apollo, I couldn't go to the grocery store without having panic attacks," says O'Brien, who served in Iraq from 2009 to 2010. "Now, I can do normal things again. I can take my kids to the park. I can go shopping. I got my life back."

The transformation didn't happen overnight. When O'Brien first returned home, she struggled with hypervigilance, insomnia, and severe anxiety in crowded places – common symptoms of PTSD that affect an estimated 11-20% of veterans who served in Operations Iraqi Freedom and Enduring Freedom, according to the Department of Veterans Affairs.

Dr. Margaret Purbrick, a clinical psychologist specializing in veteran mental health at the VA Medical Center in Boston, explains that service dogs can provide unique support that traditional treatments sometimes cannot.

"These dogs are trained to recognize signs of anxiety and distress in their handlers," says Purbrick. "They can create a physical barrier between the veteran and others in crowded spaces, wake them from nightmares, and provide a sense of security that allows veterans to engage in daily activities many of us take for granted."

The science backs this up. A recent study published in the Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology found that veterans with service dogs showed significantly lower PTSD symptoms compared to those without, including better sleep quality and reduced depression.

Rory Diamond, CEO of K9s For Warriors, says the organization has paired more than 700 veterans with service dogs since its founding in 2011, with a success rate that speaks for itself.

"We're seeing a 92% reduction in suicide rates among our graduates," Diamond reports. "These dogs aren't just pets – they're highly trained battle buddies who provide 24/7 support to veterans in crisis."

The training process is rigorous. Each service dog undergoes several months of specialized training, learning more than 100 commands specifically designed to assist veterans with PTSD. Many of the dogs come from rescue shelters, giving them a second chance at life while they help give veterans a second chance at theirs.

For Marine Corps veteran James Martinez, his service dog Duke has become an indispensable partner in his recovery journey.

"Duke knows when I'm having a bad day before I do," Martinez says. "He'll put his paw on my leg or lean against me when he senses my anxiety rising. It's like having a guardian angel who never leaves your side."

The impact extends beyond individual veterans to their families. Sarah Martinez, James's wife, has witnessed the transformation firsthand.

"Before Duke, James was withdrawn, angry, and struggled to connect with our children," she shares. "Now he's present again. He's the husband and father I remember from before his deployment."

However, access to service dogs remains a challenge for many veterans. While the PAWS Act, signed into law in 2021, created a pilot program for the VA to provide service dogs to veterans with PTSD, demand far exceeds current capacity.

Organizations like K9s For Warriors rely heavily on donations and volunteers to continue their work. The cost of training each service dog pair can exceed $25,000, but the organization provides them to veterans at no cost.

Dr. James Thompson, a researcher at the Center for the Human-Animal Bond at Purdue University, emphasizes the need for expanded access to service dogs for veterans.

"The evidence is clear that service dogs can be a valuable tool in treating PTSD," Thompson says. "What we need now is increased funding and support to make these programs available to every veteran who could benefit from them."

For O'Brien, the impact of having Apollo in her life cannot be measured in dollars and cents.

"People ask me all the time if I'm training Apollo," she says, smiling as she scratches behind her companion's ears. "I tell them he's actually training me – training me to live again, to trust again, to believe in myself again."

As more veterans like O'Brien share their success stories, the hope is that service dog programs will continue to expand, offering more veterans a chance to reclaim their lives from the invisible wounds of war.

To learn more about service dogs for veterans or to support organizations like K9s For Warriors, visit their website at k9sforwarriors.org.

In highly developed and competitive industries companies tread a continuous and very fine line between maximising shareholder profits by keeping prices up while making products as cheaply as possible, vs competitors lowering prices when they work out a way to make equivalents cheaper. In the short run you will quite often see companies hold onto large portions of efficiency savings (particularly if they make a major breakthrough in a specific manufacturing process etc) by holding old prices up, but in the long run competition pretty quickly lowers prices as the companies trying to keep high margins and prices get ruthlessly undercut by smaller competitors happy to make a bit less.

If the condom broke during sex and your partner ejaculated inside you, there is a chance that you could become pregnant. It is important to remember that sperm can live inside the female reproductive tract for up to five days, so pregnancy is still possible even if you had sex several days ago.

If you are concerned about the possibility of pregnancy, you can take a pregnancy test or speak with a healthcare provider to find out more. Pregnancy tests are most accurate when taken at least a week after a missed period. It is also a good idea to consider using emergency contraception, such as the "morning-after pill," to help reduce the risk of pregnancy.

It is important to use condoms consistently and correctly to help reduce the risk of unintended pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections (STIs). If you have had a condom break during sex, it is important to use another form of contraception, such as the pill or an IUD, and to consider getting tested for STIs.

To calculate the required rate of return for an income-generating savings account, you will need to consider the following factors:The expected return on the account: This is the amount of interest or dividends that you expect to receive from the account.The time horizon: This is the length of time over which you will be holding the account.The opportunity cost of capital: This is the return that you could have earned by investing your money in an alternative investment with similar risk.To calculate the required rate of return, you can use the following formula:Required rate of return = (Expected return - Opportunity cost of capital) / (Time horizon)For example, if you expect to receive a return of 3% per year from your income-generating savings account, and you plan to hold the account for 5 years, and the opportunity cost of capital is 2%, then your required rate of return would be:(3% - 2%) / 5 years = 0.2% per yearKeep in mind that this is just a rough estimate, and the actual required rate of return may vary depending on your specific situation and the risk involved. It is always a good idea to do your own research and consult with a financial professional before making any investment decisions.

Chest pain with breathing difficulty can have many possible causes, some of which may be serious or life-threatening. It is important to seek medical attention as soon as possible if you are experiencing chest pain and difficulty breathing, as this may be a sign of a medical emergency.

Possible causes of chest pain with breathing difficulty include:

Heart attack: Chest pain that is accompanied by difficulty breathing can be a sign of a heart attack, especially if the pain is severe and radiating to the arms, neck, or jaw. Other symptoms of a heart attack may include sweating, nausea, and dizziness.

Pulmonary embolism: A pulmonary embolism is a blockage in the artery that carries blood from the heart to the lungs. It can cause chest pain, difficulty breathing, and a rapid heart rate.

Asthma: Asthma is a respiratory condition that can cause chest pain, difficulty breathing, and wheezing.

Pneumonia: Pneumonia is an infection of the lungs that can cause chest pain, difficulty breathing, and a cough with phlegm.

Panic attack: Chest pain and difficulty breathing can also be symptoms of a panic attack, which is a sudden episode of intense fear or anxiety.

It is important to see a doctor as soon as possible if you are experiencing chest pain and difficulty breathing, as these symptoms could be a sign of a serious medical condition that requires immediate treatment. The doctor will be able to determine the cause of your symptoms and provide appropriate treatment.

The Fed is trying to keep the money supply growing at a rate just slightly faster than the increase in the total production in the economy. If this year we produced, say, 3% more goods and services than last year, than they try to make the money supply grow by maybe 4% or 5%. That way there should be a small rate of inflation. They are trying to prevent high inflation rates on one hand or deflation on the other. When the interest rate on T-bills is low, banks will borrow more money. As the Fed creates this money out of thin air when banks buy a T-bill, this adds money to the economy. When the interest rate on T-bills is high, banks will borrow little or nothing. As they'll be repaying older T-bills, this will result in less growth in the money supply or even contraction. So the Feds change the rate when they see that economic growth is accelerating or decelerating, or that the inflation rate is getting too high or too low.

If you are struggling with intrusive thoughts and they are causing you distress or interfering with your daily life, it may be helpful to seek treatment from a mental health professional. A therapist or counselor can help you learn coping strategies to manage your thoughts and improve your overall well-being.

Before 19-year-old Davontez Johnson found himself in a preschool classroom at Dorothy I. Heights Elementary, he was a senior at a nearby high school who, like many students his age, was unsure of what he wanted to do with his life. Not in his wildest dreams could he have imagined himself standing on a colorful carpet, leading a gaggle of 4-year-olds in a chant and dance about phonics.

“Words have parts — that’s syl-a-bles,” he said, enunciating for effect. The preschoolers craned their heads up at Johnson and echoed him. “Clap your hands now, syl-a-bles! Stomp your feet now, syl-a-bles!”

Johnson is part of the Leading Men Fellowship, which trains young Black and Latino men to become early literacy instructors in preschool classrooms across the country. It’s a program that aims to tackle several problems at once: a shortage of early educators, a dearth of Black and Latino male teachers and the acute challenges boys of color face in schools because of their race and gender.

“We’re not only affecting change in the classroom with these school students, but (we’re) also developing these young future educators,” said Ivan Douglas of the Literacy Lab, which runs the Leading Men Fellowship.

Many fellows, like Johnson, are recruited right out of high school. After an interview process and intensive summer training, they go to work in schools where they may be among the only male educators. Fellows make between $16.50 and $18 an hour.

A former high school offensive lineman, Johnson knows some parents would say he looks out of place in a preschool classroom. And the statistics back him up: Less than 1% of elementary and early education public school teachers are Black men, according to federal data. But that’s part of the reason he wanted to do it.

“I really thought it was a great opportunity. Because I know if I saw someone like me, you know, in pre-K, I’d be pretty excited,” Johnson said. “You don’t see a lot of young Black males.”

Researchers have shown that Black male students encounter discrimination before they even set foot in a kindergarten classroom, facing higher rates of expulsion and suspension from preschool even though evidence suggests they do not misbehave more than their white peers. Boys also are far more likely than girls to be expelled.

But there’s a growing body of evidence that Black teachers can make a difference for Black students — and for Black boys in particular. In the years since the Leading Men Fellowship was founded, in 2016, researchers have repeatedly found that students of color seem to fare better when they have teachers who look like them.

Johns Hopkins University economist Nicholas Papageorge, who is based not far from Heights Elementary, studies the impact of Black teachers on Black students. His research found that Black teachers have higher expectations for Black students than do non-Black teachers.

“If a Black student had a white teacher and a Black teacher, that white teacher had systematically lower expectations,” Papageorge said.

His later research found Black students who have a Black teacher are less likely to drop out of high school and more likely to attend college. The effect of having a Black teacher had the greatest impact on Black boys from low-income households.

Through his coursework, Johnson has learned the intricacies of early education — and that it involves a surprising amount of singing and dancing for someone not working on Broadway. Children learn best by repetition, and when they can pair information with movements and song.

Bridget Jeffrys, whose preschool classroom hosts Johnson, said she had never worked alongside a male educator until Johnson arrived at the start of the last school year. She said she’s watched Johnson grow more confident with her students, going from reserved to enthusiastic. Jeffrys said his voice and dance moves could use some work, but he performs the songs with such heart that it doesn’t matter.

“It was so beautiful because usually you don’t see men really get down to the child level,” Jeffrys said. “That excited them even more. A lot of kids think he’s a big kid.”

Along with teaching at Heights Elementary, Johnson is studying political science at University of Maryland Global Campus and hopes to go into politics. His colleagues, though, are encouraging him to stick with teaching.

While Johnson is there to provide targeted literacy instruction, he has been fully integrated into the school day. His second week in the classroom, he sang the class’s morning greeting song in a robot voice. When a child is squirming on the carpet or wandering away from story time, Johnson is there to rein them in.

On this October day, Johnson pulled students aside to help them work on writing their names. He had only been with this cohort for a couple weeks, but many students were drawn to him. During free-play time, he encouraged a student who was working on a crayon rubbing of a leaf.

“You’ve done a wonderful job,” he said to the girl, who stared up at him, eager for reassurance. Another student interrupted him by handing him a fistful of play money.

After lunchtime, as most of the preschoolers sat on the carpet held rapt by a story read by Jeffrys, 4-year-old Kodi Hendricks wandered toward the door and peered into the hallway until Johnson beckoned him back. Johnson bent his large frame to tie the boy’s shoe and then they sat together for a penmanship lesson.

“What’s the first letter?” he asked the boy.

“K,” he replied. Johnson showed him, in slow motion, how to draw a K.

“No, I can’t do it,” said the boy.

“It’s all right,” Johnson said. He urged him on.

“You can do it. It just takes practice.”

In a scrubby patch of rainforest in central Panama, a small brown frog with bright speckles has begun doing something biologists weren’t sure they’d ever see again: surviving in numbers. Several years back, nearly every amphibian here seemed doomed. A deadly fungal pathogen called **Batrachochytrium dendrobatidis**, or Bd for short, had slashed local frog populations by as much as 90 percent. Species that were once abundant along streamsides and leaf-strewn trails vanished almost overnight. Now, despite ongoing infections, a handful of survivors are croaking and courting again. The mere sight of them gives researchers reason to believe that certain frogs can evolve resistance—or at least tolerance—to a fungus long feared to be unstoppable.

**A Global Killer on the Move**  
Bd emerged as a global threat in the late 20th century, ravaging amphibians on nearly every continent except Antarctica. By the early 2000s, the fungus had contributed to declines or extinctions of over 500 species, making it one of the most destructive pathogens documented in wildlife. It reproduces in a frog’s skin, interfering with fluid balance and leading to cardiac arrest. It doesn’t help that frogs absorb water and salts directly through their skin, so the fungus essentially wrecks their most vital interface with the environment. For many years, scientists struggled to find any bright spots amid the carnage.

“There were a few holdouts, but the story was grim,” says Dr. Karen Lips, a biologist at the University of Maryland who witnessed the fungus’s devastating impact in Panama. “We’d arrive at streams we knew were full of frogs just a year before, and find almost nothing left alive.” She and her colleagues suspected that if any amphibians were to persist, they’d have to adapt quickly—either physiologically or through changes in behavior or skin chemistry.

**Signs of Resistance and Resilience**  
Recent evidence suggests some frogs are indeed fighting back. Researchers led by Dr. Jamie Voyles, an ecologist at the University of Nevada, Reno, have shown that certain populations, once hard hit, are stabilizing or even rebounding. The survivors aren’t merely lucky individuals who avoided infection; instead, some frogs can now carry Bd on their skin without succumbing. In one study published in *Science*, Voyles and her team identified changes in the frogs’ immune responses, including more potent antimicrobial peptides—tiny molecules in their skin that zap pathogens.

“There’s a shift in how these frogs’ immune systems function,” says Voyles. “We’re seeing differences in the composition of their skin microbiome, too—beneficial bacteria that might help fend off the fungus.” These alterations aren’t dramatic superpowers. They’re subtle changes spread across populations, but they could mean the difference between extinction and survival.

It’s not just about skin defenses. Some frogs may now regulate their body temperatures more strategically. Others might choose microhabitats that are less conducive to the fungus’s growth. The result is that at least a few species are coexisting with Bd rather than being obliterated by it. “We’ve gone from disaster mode—‘All these amphibians are doomed’—to recognizing that nature sometimes comes up with remarkable solutions,” Lips says.

**New Tools to Tip the Balance**  
Even with these glimmers of hope, frogs can use some help. Some scientists are testing approaches to give amphibians a leg up. One idea is to seed frog habitats with beneficial microbes—bacteria that can slow the fungus’s spread. Another involves carefully targeted antifungal treatments in certain breeding areas. In places like Panama and Costa Rica, researchers have also tried reintroducing captive-bred frogs, hoping that controlled conditions might allow them to mature with stronger defenses before facing Bd in the wild.

Zoos and labs are refining treatments like “probiotic baths,” which involve soaking frogs in water teeming with protective microbes. “It’s not a silver bullet,” says Dr. Luke Linhoff, a wildlife veterinarian with the Panama Amphibian Rescue and Conservation Project. “But if we can boost their natural defenses, we may give them that extra margin they need.” He notes that even minor improvements in survival odds can help species struggling to gain a foothold after catastrophic declines.

In addition, some teams are using genetic tools to understand precisely which genes change when frogs become more tolerant. By decoding these pathways, scientists hope to identify markers of resistance that could guide conservation strategies. If they know which populations carry these promising traits, they can prioritize habitats and shield them from logging or pollution. None of these interventions guarantee success, but they offer options beyond watchful despair.

**Adjusting to a New Normal**  
Today, Bd remains a massive threat. Many amphibian species haven’t yet shown signs of bouncing back. Some that were common are functionally extinct in the wild. Others persist only in carefully guarded breeding centers. Still, the evolving defenses of certain frogs provide a blueprint for what recovery might look like. It won’t be a simple return to the past: the amphibian communities of tomorrow may be different in composition and behavior, and researchers must accept a certain amount of trial-and-error in their interventions.

Despite the uncertainties, Lips is encouraged by what she’s seen in recent field seasons. “When we first came face-to-face with this fungus, it seemed insurmountable,” she says. “But we’re finally seeing frogs that have learned to live alongside it.” Around the rainforest streams and mossy boulders where Bd first announced itself so catastrophically, at least a few amphibians are forging a future—even if that future looks unlike anything we’ve known before.

Utilities and cost of living vary from city to city but maybe not that much.  For basic planning purposes you can probably figure to spend as much as you are now, maybe a little more.  And adjust as needed when you get there.  (And adjust if, for example, you're moving from a very low cost of living area or to a very high cost of living area.) The cost of housing varies quite a bit from city to city, but you can do this research using Zillow, Craigslist, other places. Now, on to moving itself.  The cost of moving can vary hugely depending on how much stuff you have and how much work you want to do.  On the cheap end, you can rent a U-Haul or one of those portable boxes that they plant outside your old house and move for you.  You'll do all the packing/loading/unloading/unpacking yourself but it saves quite a bit of money.  My family and I moved from Seattle to California last year using one of those portable box places and it ended up costing us ~$1400 including 30 days of storage at the destination while we looked for a place.  We have a <1000 sq foot place with some furniture but not a huge amount and did all the packing/loading ourselves.  If we had wanted full service where people come pack, load, unpack, etc, it could have been 2-3x that amount.  (And if we had more stuff, it could have been a lot more expensive too.  Try not to acquire too much stuff as you just end up having to move it around and take care of it all!)  Your employer may cover moving expenses, ask about this when talking about job offers.  Un-reimbursed moving expenses are tax-deductible in the US (even if you don't itemize).   Since you're just starting out, your best bet is to overestimate how much you think things will cost, then adjust as you arrive and settle in for a few months.  Try to save as much as you can, but remember to have fun too.  Hope this helps!

Getting the first year right for any rental property is key. It is even more complex when you rent a room, or rent via a service like AirBnB. Get professional tax advice. For you the IRS rules are covered in Tax Topic 415 Renting Residential and Vacation Property and IRS pub 527 Residential Rental Property There is a special rule if you use a dwelling unit as a personal   residence and rent it for fewer than 15 days. In this case, do not   report any of the rental income and do not deduct any expenses as   rental expenses. If you reach that reporting threshold the IRS will now expect you to to have to report the income, and address the items such as depreciation. When you go to sell the house you will again have to address depreciation. All of this adds complexity to your tax situation. The best advice is to make sure that in a tax year you don't cross that threshold. When you have a house that is part personal residence, and part rental property some parts of the tax code become complex. You will have to divide all the expenses (mortgage, property tax, insurance) and split it between the two uses. You will also have to take that rental portion of the property and depreciation it. You will need to determine the value of the property before the split and then determine the value of the rental portion at the time of the split. From then on, you will follow the IRS regulations for depreciation of the rental portion until you either convert it back to non-rental or sell the property.  When the property is sold the portion of the sales price will be associated with the rental property, and you will need to determine if the rental property is sold for a profit or a loss. You will also have to recapture the depreciation. It is possible that one portion of the property could show a loss, and the other part of the property a gain depending on house prices over the decades. You can expect that AirBnB will collect tax info and send it to the IRS As a US company, we’re required by US law to collect taxpayer   information from hosts who appear to have US-sourced income. Virginia will piggyback onto the IRS rules. Local law must be researched because they may limit what type of rentals are allowed. Local law could be state, or county/city/town. Even zoning regulations could apply. Also check any documents from your Home Owners Association, they may address running a business or renting a property.  You may need to adjust your insurance policy regarding having tenants. You may also want to look at insurance to protect you if a renter is injured.

The Federal Reserve, or the Fed, is the central bank of the United States and is responsible for implementing monetary policy in the country. One of the tools the Fed has at its disposal to influence the supply of money in the economy is the ability to print new money. However, the Fed does not actually "print" physical cash in the way that the U.S. Treasury does. Instead, the Fed creates new money electronically, by creating new reserves in the banking system and purchasing securities from banks or other financial institutions.The Fed can use this power to increase the money supply in order to achieve its policy objectives, such as stabilizing prices and promoting full employment. For example, if the Fed wants to stimulate economic growth, it can create new money and use it to purchase securities, such as government bonds or mortgage-backed securities, from banks. This increases the reserves of the banks, which they can then use to make new loans to households and businesses. This can lead to an increase in spending, which can help stimulate economic growth.The Fed can also use this power to reduce the money supply in order to achieve its policy objectives. For example, if the Fed wants to reduce inflation, it can sell securities from its portfolio, which reduces the reserves of the banks and reduces the amount of money available for lending. This can help reduce spending and bring down inflation.Overall, the Fed's ability to create new money is an important tool for implementing monetary policy and achieving its policy objectives. However, it is important to note that the Fed must carefully balance the benefits of using this power with the potential risks, such as the risk of inflation or financial instability.

In a fascinating discovery that has left marine biologists intrigued, two bowhead whales separated by roughly 60 miles of Arctic waters were observed diving in near-perfect synchronization, raising new questions about these mysterious creatures' communication abilities and social behaviors.

The unexpected finding came during a long-term study of bowhead whale movements in the Canadian Arctic, where researchers from the University of British Columbia had attached sophisticated tracking devices to multiple whales to monitor their diving patterns and migration routes.

"We were absolutely stunned when we analyzed the data," says Dr. Sarah Matthews, lead author of the study published in Marine Mammal Science. "Two whales, which we named Whale A and Whale B, were repeatedly diving and surfacing at almost exactly the same times, despite being at distances where they couldn't possibly see each other."

The tracking devices recorded that over a 12-hour period, both whales executed similar diving patterns, with each dive lasting between 15 to 20 minutes and surface intervals occurring within seconds of each other. This level of synchronization is unprecedented at such distances in marine mammals.

Bowhead whales, which can grow to lengths of up to 60 feet and live for more than 200 years, are known for their powerful vocalizations. These whales can produce complex songs that can travel long distances underwater, thanks to the excellent sound-conducting properties of cold Arctic waters.

Dr. William Thompson, a marine biologist at the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution who wasn't involved in the study, explains: "Sound travels about four times faster in water than in air, and in the cold, dense Arctic waters, it can travel even further with less degradation. But even with these optimal conditions, coordinated behavior at 60 miles apart is remarkable."

The research team believes that the whales might have been using low-frequency vocalizations to communicate and coordinate their diving behavior. Bowhead whales can produce sounds at frequencies as low as 10 Hz, which can potentially travel hundreds of miles under optimal conditions.

"These low-frequency calls are like the bass notes in music," says Dr. Matthews. "They can penetrate through water masses and potentially carry information about the whale's location, behavior, and possibly even their intentions."

The synchronization might serve several purposes. One theory suggests it could be a feeding strategy, with whales coordinating their dives to track and exploit patches of prey across vast distances. Another possibility is that it's a social behavior, helping maintain connections between members of the same population even when they're far apart.

Dr. Elena Rodriguez, a whale behavior specialist at the Norwegian Polar Institute, offers another perspective: "This could be evidence of a much more sophisticated communication network among bowhead whales than we previously understood. They might be sharing information about food sources, ice conditions, or potential dangers across vast distances."

The discovery has implications for whale conservation efforts, particularly in the Arctic, where climate change and increasing human activity are altering the acoustic environment. "If bowhead whales are indeed communicating over such large distances, we need to be particularly mindful of noise pollution from shipping, oil exploration, and other human activities that could disrupt these communications," warns Dr. Thompson.

The research team is now expanding their study to include more whales and longer observation periods. They're also developing more advanced recording equipment to capture the actual vocalizations that might be facilitating this synchronized behavior.

"We're just scratching the surface of understanding the complexity of whale communication and social networks," says Dr. Matthews. "These animals have been evolving for millions of years in an environment where sound is the primary means of communication. It's likely they've developed capabilities that we're only beginning to comprehend."

The study also highlights the importance of considering larger spatial scales when studying marine mammal behavior. Traditional observation methods, which typically focus on visible surface behaviors or interactions between nearby individuals, might be missing important aspects of these animals' social lives.

Dr. Rodriguez adds, "This finding reminds us that marine mammals don't experience their environment the way we do. Their acoustic world is vast and complex, and what we consider to be 'far apart' might not be so distant in their perception."

As research continues, scientists hope to better understand the mechanisms behind this synchronized behavior and its significance in bowhead whale ecology. This knowledge could prove crucial for protecting these magnificent creatures and their acoustic environment in an increasingly noisy ocean.

The study serves as another reminder of the remarkable capabilities of marine mammals and how much we still have to learn about their lives beneath the waves. As human activities continue to impact marine environments, understanding these complex behaviors becomes increasingly important for conservation efforts.

Upstream is into businesses that supply the original business; downstream is into businesses that make use of the original product.  So in that description, what they are saying is that the original business received products from plantations and sent products to manufacturing. This is also called vertical integration.  Meaning that they are diversifying along their supply chain so that they control more of it.  This is in contrast with horizontal integration, where they move into new products that either compete with the existing products or which are entirely separate.   In general, the upside of vertical integration is that a company is less reliant on suppliers (and intermediate consumers) and has more control over its supply chain.  The downside is that they have less opportunity to partner with other companies in the same supply chain, as they compete with them.  Some companies are better at managing to do both.  For example, Amazon.com has integrated fulfillment and sales.  But partners can still do their own fulfillment and/or sales, choosing how much to send out to Amazon.   If you are investing in individual stocks, integrated companies can be problematic in that they cut across diversification areas.  So they can be harder to balance with other stocks.  You can either buy plantations, transport, and manufacturing together or not buy at all.  If your investment strategy says to increase plantations and reduce manufacturing, this can be difficult to implement with an integrated company.  Of course, everyone else has the same problem, which can lead to integrated companies being undervalued.  So they may be an opportunity as a value stock.

In a groundbreaking move, California has enacted new legislation aimed at safeguarding the financial futures of child influencers. The law, which will take effect in January, mandates that parents and guardians who profit from social media posts featuring their children must set aside a portion of the earnings for the young stars themselves. This development marks a significant step in addressing the growing concerns over the exploitation of minors in the digital age.

The rise of social media platforms like Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube has given birth to a new generation of child influencers, some of whom boast millions of followers and lucrative brand deals. "These children are working, and they deserve to have their earnings protected just like any other child actor or performer," Skinner said. "This law ensures that they have a financial safety net for their future."

The legislation draws inspiration from the Coogan Law, which was enacted in the 1930s to protect child actors in Hollywood. Named after child actor Jackie Coogan, who famously lost his earnings to his parents, the Coogan Law requires a portion of a child actor's earnings to be set aside in a trust. The new law extends similar protections to child influencers, recognizing the parallels between traditional entertainment and the burgeoning world of social media.

Experts in child labor and digital media have praised the legislation as a necessary step in adapting to the evolving landscape of work and entertainment. In response to such concerns, the law includes provisions for financial literacy resources and support for families navigating the new requirements. The state plans to collaborate with financial institutions to ensure that setting up and managing trust accounts is as seamless as possible.

The legislation also raises broader questions about the ethics of involving children in social media content creation. Critics argue that the pressure to maintain a public persona can be detrimental to a child's development and well-being. Dr. Emily Carter, a child psychologist, cautioned, "While financial protections are crucial, we must also consider the psychological impact of social media fame on young children. As the law takes effect, it is expected to influence similar legislative efforts in other states and potentially at the federal level. Advocates hope that it will set a precedent for protecting the rights of child influencers across the country.

In the meantime, California's new law represents a significant step forward in ensuring that the digital economy is fair and equitable for its youngest participants. Globally, invasive species are increasingly problematic, endangering biodiversity, disturbing ecosystems, and leading to considerable economic harm. Conventional approaches to managing these species typically use chemicals or physical removal, which may unintentionally damage the environment. Nonetheless, new methods involving detection dogs, toads, and artificial intelligence (AI) are proving to be successful and eco-friendly options.

The Benefit of Using Dogs

Dogs, renowned for their exceptional olfactory abilities, are now being utilized to identify invasive species. These "detective dogs" are trained to locate particular plants, animals, or their eggs by scent, making them crucial for early detection initiatives.

Pete Coppolillo, the Executive Director of Working Dogs for Conservation, states that dogs are capable of rapidly surveying extensive areas and identifying species that are challenging to locate by other means. Their skill in detecting invasive species even when they are scarce makes them an invaluable asset in conservation efforts.

In Florida, for example, dogs have effectively been employed to find Burmese pythons, an invasive species that significantly endangers local wildlife. Detecting these snakes at an early stage allows for their removal before they can establish a larger population.

Utilizing Toads as Biological Control Agents

In certain ecosystems, indigenous species can be used to manage invasive populations. In some regions, toads are employed to control populations of invasive insects. These amphibians naturally prey on numerous insects, helping to regulate their populations without relying on chemical pesticides.

Dr. Emily Johnson, a herpetologist at the University of California, observes that toads play a crucial role in various ecosystems and offer an eco-friendly method for managing invasive insect populations. By bolstering native predator numbers, we can preserve ecological equilibrium and lessen the dependence on damaging chemicals.

It's important to make sure that promoting or introducing native predators doesn't unintentionally cause new ecological issues. Thorough observation and study are crucial to confirm that these initiatives are advantageous and do not interfere with current ecosystems.

Leveraging Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence is transforming conservation efforts by providing innovative tools for tracking and controlling invasive species. AI has the capability to swiftly process large datasets, recognizing trends and forecasting the proliferation of invasive species with impressive precision.

Dr. Sarah Thompson, an expert in ecological data science, describes how AI enables the analysis of satellite images, climate information, and species distribution models to forecast potential spread areas for invasive species. This data is essential for determining priority areas for action and efficiently distributing resources.

A notable use of AI is in controlling invasive plant species. AI algorithms can detect regions where invasive plants are spreading into native habitats by examining satellite imagery. This enables conservationists to focus their efforts more accurately, minimizing effects on unintended species and environments.

A Cooperative Strategy

The most successful approach to managing invasive species typically involves integrating various methods, as each offers distinct benefits. By combining the advantages of detection dogs, toads, and AI, conservationists can create holistic management strategies that are effective and eco-friendly.

Pete Coppolillo highlights the necessity of working together, noting that "no single approach is a perfect solution." By integrating various methods and collaborating, we can build stronger ecosystems and safeguard biodiversity for the generations to come.

Obstacles and Prospective Paths

Even with the potential of these new techniques, obstacles still exist. Considerable resources are needed to train and deploy detection dogs, and the management of native predators must be handled with care to prevent unforeseen impacts. Moreover, although AI provides robust predictive and analytical capabilities, it depends on high-quality data, which can be challenging to acquire in isolated or less-researched regions.

Future progress will require ongoing research and funding for these technologies. Enhancing and broadening the use of these techniques will strengthen our capacity to control invasive species and safeguard global biodiversity.

In summary, addressing invasive species is a challenging and continuous effort. By adopting novel strategies such as detection dogs, toads, and AI, we can create more efficient and lasting solutions. As we advance our understanding and adaptability, these approaches provide optimism for a future with more robust and thriving ecosystems.

A San Francisco startup aiming to help dogs live longer, healthier lives has just raised $45 million in funding, highlighting a growing interest among venture-capital firms in longevity technologies—this time, not just for humans. “We love our dogs like family members,” says Celine Halioua, Loyal’s founder and CEO, “but they simply don’t live as long as we want them to. At Loyal, we’re trying to address the underlying biology of aging so that our pets can enjoy more happy and active years with us.”

Founded in 2019, Loyal has drawn attention from high-profile investors as the pet industry continues to expand. According to the American Pet Products Association, Americans spend more than $100 billion a year on their pets, reflecting a strong appetite for products and services that improve animal health and longevity. With this latest round of funding, Loyal plans to continue its research, run clinical trials, and prepare the groundwork for bringing its first products to market.

The startup’s core idea is to develop pharmaceuticals that target the biological mechanisms of aging. Instead of addressing one disease at a time—such as arthritis or heart conditions—Loyal hopes to treat aging itself as a risk factor for multiple diseases. If successful, the drugs could extend not only the length of dogs’ lives, but also the quality of those extra years.

Dr. Matt Kaeberlein, a longevity researcher at the University of Washington who is not affiliated with Loyal, notes that the concept of treating aging as a medical condition is gaining traction in the scientific community. “The past decade has shown us that aging is modifiable,” he says. “If we can slow down the aging process, we may be able to significantly reduce the incidence of age-related diseases. Doing this for dogs is an appealing and achievable first step, given their relatively short lifespans and the strength of owner interest.”

Venture-capital investors have been paying close attention. While several longevity startups focus on human aging, the pet market offers a unique entry point. Dogs have shorter lifespans than people, meaning that clinical trials can yield data more quickly. The pet health market is also less strictly regulated than human pharmaceuticals, potentially speeding up the time it takes for a product to reach consumers. “Investors see an opportunity to generate returns while contributing to a growing field with vast potential,” says Mark Davies, a biotech investment analyst.

Loyal’s funding round places it among a cohort of longevity-focused startups that have recently raised significant capital. These companies aim to tap into a future where therapies could prevent or slow degenerative conditions across species. Some industry watchers believe that if these therapies are successful in dogs, the lessons learned could guide similar approaches for human medicine. “There’s a lot we can learn about aging from animal models,” Dr. Kaeberlein explains. “Dogs share our environment and many of our health risks, making them an ideal species to study.”

Still, the journey from concept to commercialization is long. Drug development is fraught with uncertainty, clinical trials can take years, and not every promising idea leads to a safe and effective product. Loyal must navigate a complex web of scientific, regulatory, and market challenges. “It’s one thing to prove something works in a laboratory setting,” says Davies, “and another to demonstrate safety, efficacy, and reliability at scale.”

For now, Loyal’s investors remain optimistic. The funding round, led by prominent venture firms, suggests that even with the known challenges, the company’s approach resonates with those holding the purse strings. “We look for investments that can reshape markets,” says an unnamed investor involved in the deal. “If Loyal’s approach pans out, it could fundamentally change how we think about pet health and aging.”

In the meantime, pet owners eagerly follow these developments. While it may be several years before a longevity treatment hits store shelves or veterinarians’ offices, the idea that science could help extend the time we spend with our furry friends is appealing. “Dogs bring us so much joy,” says Halioua. “Why not give them the healthiest, longest lives we can?”

As research continues, Loyal’s latest funding round signals a broader shift in how we view aging—not just as an inevitable decline, but as a biological process we might someday influence. For dogs, and perhaps one day for humans, that shift could mean more vibrant years together.

A spacecraft blasted off Monday to investigate the scene of a cosmic crash. 

The European Space Agency’s Hera spacecraft rocketed away on a two-year journey to the small, harmless asteroid rammed by NASA two years ago in a dress rehearsal for the day a killer space rock threatens Earth. It’s the second part of a planetary defense test that could one day help save the planet. 

SpaceX’s Falcon rocket quickly disappeared with Hera into the late morning clouds. An hour later, applause erupted in the control center in Germany as the spacecraft separated from the rocket’s upper stage and then called home. “It’s an amazing day,” the space agency’s director general Josef Aschbacher said afterward. 

The 2022 crash by NASA’s Dart spacecraft shortened Dimorphos’ orbit around its bigger companion, demonstrating that if a dangerous rock was headed our way, there’s a chance it could be knocked off course with enough advance notice. 

Scientists are eager to examine the impact’s aftermath up close to know exactly how effective Dart was and what changes might be needed to safeguard Earth in the future. 

“The more detail we can glean the better as it may be important for planning a future deflection mission should one be needed,” University of Maryland astronomer Derek Richardson said before launch. 

Researchers want to know whether Dart — short for Double Asteroid Redirection Test — left a crater or perhaps reshaped the 500-foot (150-meter) asteroid more dramatically. It looked something like a flying saucer before Dart’s blow and may now resemble a kidney bean, said Richardson, who took part in the Dart mission and is helping with Hera. 

Dart’s wallop sent rubble and even boulders flying off Dimorphos, providing an extra kick to the impact’s momentum. The debris trail extended thousands of miles (more than 10,000 kilometers) into space for months. 

Some boulders and other debris could still be hanging around the asteroid, posing a potential threat to Hera, said flight director Ignacio Tanco. 

“We don’t really know very well the environment in which we are going to operate,” said Tanco. “But that’s the whole point of the mission is to go there and find out.” 

European officials describe the $400 million (363 million euro) mission as a “crash scene investigation.” 

Hera “is going back to the crime site and getting all the scientific and technical information,” said project manager Ian Carnelli. 

Carrying a dozen science instruments, the small car-sized Hera will need to swing past Mars in 2025 for a gravity boost, before arriving at Dimorphos by the end of 2026. It’s a moonlet of Didymos, Greek for twin, a fast-spinning asteroid that’s five times bigger. At that time, the asteroids will be 120 million miles (195 million kilometers) from Earth. 

Hera will attempt to go into orbit around the rocky pair, with the flyby distances gradually dropping from 18 miles (30 kilometers) all the way down to a half-mile (1 kilometer). The spacecraft will survey the moonlet for at least six months to ascertain its mass, shape and composition, as well as its orbit around Didymos. 

Before the impact, Dimorphos circled its larger companion from three-quarters of a mile (1,189 meters) out. Scientists believe the orbit is now tighter and oval-shaped, and that the moonlet may even be tumbling. 

Two shoebox-sized Cubesats will pop off Hera for even closer drone-like inspections, with one of them using radar to peer beneath the moonlet’s boulder-strewn surface. Scientists suspect Dimorphos was formed from material shed from Didymos. The radar observations should help confirm whether Didymos is indeed the little moon’s parent. 

The Cubesats will attempt to land on the moonlet once their survey is complete. If the moonlet is tumbling, that will complicate the endeavor. Hera may also end its mission with a precarious touchdown, but on the larger Didymos. 

Neither asteroid poses any threat to Earth — before or after Dart showed up. That’s why NASA picked the pair for humanity’s first asteroid-deflecting demo. 

Leftovers from the solar system’s formation 4.6 billion years ago, asteroids primarily orbit the sun between Mars and Jupiter in what’s known as the main asteroid belt, where millions of them reside. They become near-Earth objects when they’re knocked out of the belt and into our neck of the woods. 

NASA’s near-Earth object count currently tops 36,000, almost all asteroids but also some comets. More than 2,400 of them are considered potentially hazardous to Earth.

The animal kingdom offers a captivating range when it comes to taste. The variety is remarkable, from animals with exceptional taste abilities to those that hardly perceive flavors. Recognizing these variations not only underscores how animals have adapted to their habitats but also provides clues about the evolutionary journeys that have influenced their sensory perceptions.

The Extraordinary Taste Abilities of the Catfish

Leading the taste spectrum is the catfish, an animal that can be regarded as a genuine expert in flavors. The catfish possesses the most advanced taste sense among animals, boasting more than 100,000 taste buds distributed all over its body. This extraordinary capability enables the catfish to locate food in cloudy waters with limited visibility. "A marine biologist describes catfish as being akin to mobile tongues." "Their enhanced taste sensitivity is vital for thriving in settings where other senses may not function as well."

Taste buds in catfish are spread across their skin, fins, and whisker-like barbels, rather than being limited to their mouth. This vast array of taste receptors allows the catfish to sense tiny chemical variations in the water, directing it accurately to possible food sources.

Dolphins and Their Lack of Taste Sensation

In stark contrast, dolphins possess a surprisingly underdeveloped sense of taste. In contrast to catfish, dolphins have evolved to lose the majority of their taste receptors. According to a marine mammal expert, dolphins depend mainly on their sharp hearing and echolocation for hunting and navigation. "Their taste buds are greatly diminished because taste is not essential for them."

Dolphins can still detect salt, crucial for keeping their electrolyte levels stable, but they do not have receptors for sweet, bitter, and umami tastes. This diminished sense of taste is believed to be an adaptation to their life in water, where other senses take precedence over taste.

Hummingbirds' Preference for Sweetness

Conversely, hummingbirds have developed a unique preference for sweet flavors. These small birds possess specialized taste receptors that are highly sensitive to sugar, essential for supporting their energetic way of life. "Hummingbirds need a continuous supply of energy due to their high metabolic rate," an ornithologist notes. "Their capacity to detect and favor sweet nectar is an ideal adaptation to meet their energy requirements."

Remarkably, hummingbirds have adapted their savory taste receptors to sense sweetness, highlighting a unique evolutionary change that emphasizes the crucial role of sugar in their diet. This adaptation enables them to effectively find and ingest the nectar that fuels their swift wing movements and vigorous flying.

The Harsh Reality for Plant-Eaters

Plant-eating animals like cows and horses possess a keen sense of taste, especially when it comes to detecting bitter flavors. This heightened taste sensitivity aids them in steering clear of poisonous plants, which frequently have a bitter flavor. "A zoologist explains that for herbivores, recognizing bitterness is vital for their survival." "It serves as a natural safeguard against ingesting toxic materials."

These animals possess a wide array of taste receptors that enable them to detect slight variations in plant flavors, helping them choose nutritious and safe foods. Their taste buds serve not just for pleasure but as an essential part of their feeding approach.

The Limited Taste Range of Chickens

Unlike other animals, chickens have a rather limited ability to taste. They have approximately 24 taste buds, making them much less sensitive to flavors than many other animals. A poultry scientist notes that chickens depend more on their vision and tactile sense while searching for food. "Their restricted sense of taste aligns with their eating patterns, which prioritize accessibility over flavor."

Even with their few taste buds, chickens are capable of sensing specific flavors like salt and sour, which influence how they feed. Nonetheless, they primarily concentrate on the physical attributes of food, including its texture and size.

To sum up, animals exhibit a diverse and intricate sense of taste, molded by evolutionary forces and their environmental requirements. From the catfish's extensive taste abilities to the dolphins' restricted flavor perception, each species has tailored its taste senses to fit its distinct way of living. Grasping these distinctions enhances our comprehension of animal biology and underscores the remarkable variety of life on Earth.

When David Lane first started teaching, one of his students called him "Humpty Dumpty." That was enough for the high-school art instructor in Rochester, N.Y., to swap his low-slung pants, held up with suspenders, for ones that hit higher. Though it felt like a small adjustment, Lane found the altered shape a big confidence booster. "It lengthens your legs," said the 45-year-old, who stands at 5'10. "It makes me feel taller."

He didn't yet know it, but Lane was embracing the "rule of thirds," a Hollywood styling trick that dictates that a man's shirt or sweater should cover the upper third of his body, and his pants fill out the lower two. The goal: to mimic the classic proportions of old-school movie-star garb—think Cary Grant's tailored slacks from the '50s that, with their higher-rise, fastened neatly around the navel. "It looks sharp," said British designer Charlie Casely-Hayford, noting that no matter one's body type, the technique helps "balance it out."

Casely-Hayford considers the "rule of thirds" to be a cousin to art's "Golden Ratio," which holds that in a painting, visual harmony is achieved when smaller sections are in specific proportion to larger ones—much like the sections of an outfit. "It applies some of that traditional compositional thinking" to a look, he explained. Still, you needn't be a wonk to work out how high to hoist your pants: "It's generally the natural waist point, around the belly button," he said.

This idea might be based on age-old geometry, but it has modern fans. Celebrities like Donald Glover, Paul Mescal and Harry Styles now play by the rule in higher-waisted trousers with tucked tops. The style hack has also gone viral: TikTok videos tagged with "rule of thirds" have been viewed more than five million times.

But though the technique is trendy, it's not exactly easy. "You have to know your proportions," explained London stylist Eric Down, who works with stars like Chris Hemsworth and Henry Cavill. Added Sean Dixon, the co-founder of Savile Row tailor Richard James, "There's a definite balance to be struck, depending on the individual figure."

That's especially true for men with rounder builds. Casely-Hayford noted that clients with "a slight paunch" should find pants that hit just above the belly button. "Nearly every time, that really flatters their shape."

"If your pants hit at the widest point of your stomach, they can draw attention to that," said Down. For huskier bodies, he recommends pairing such pants with a jacket or button-up that falls a little lower, just above the hip, which "draws the eye down."

Bryan O'Sullivan, 42, an interior designer based in London and New York, said that along with "pulling in the tummy," the technique helps his backside seem more toned, especially with darker denim or crisp khaki, which drapes nicely across the curve of the lower torso. "It gives you a good bum," he said.

For best results, consider slacks with straight, slightly wider legs . "Pants tend to fall cleaner when they're cut straight," said Peter Zottolo, 48, a photographer from San Francisco, who recommends khakis from J.Crew and denim from Ben Davis. Stylist Down said pants in thicker fabrics, such as the trousers by British designer Nigel Cabourn, "fall better with a bit of weight." Skinny belts help add some subtle definition between the waist and chest.

As for tops, consider shorter, even boxier shapes . Buck Mason and Lady White Co. make shirts with slightly abbreviated hems. An unexpected jacket can also make the proportions more modern. O'Sullivan layers a cropped, colorful Bode jacket over a tightly tucked white tee and wide-leg trousers, "which gives it a spin."

He also adds rubber clogs, like those from Simone Rocha, for a contemporary edge. Even though the silhouette riffs on old movies, O'Sullivan said, "you don't want to actually dress like a person from the 1940s."

Fans of the "rule of thirds" admit that some mental recalibration is needed to adopt the technique. "It does feel a bit odd the first time you do it," said Lane, the high-school teacher. But now that he's in the high-waisted club, he says he can't go back. "I just wore a pair of lower waisted, slim-fitting pants that I always thought looked great," he said. But after seeing himself in photos, Lane realized those low-slung pants now seemed dated. "I've changed gears. They just felt wrong."

Yes, from June 1968 until December 1968, they closed the NYSE every Wednesday so they could catch up on paperwork representing billions of dollars in unprocessed transactions.  Even after the NYSE re-opened on Wednesdays in January 1969, they still had to close it early at 2pm for seven more months. Forbes has a description of this: Not to be forgotten, though, is the Paperwork Crunch. In a day of email and the Cloud and trading completed in microseconds, the idea that Wall Street needed Wednesdays off in the late 1960′s to catch up on back-office tasks seems especially quaint. Yet, in 1968, the NYSE found itself sitting on more than $4 billion in unprocessed transactions. Trading had risen to 21 million shares daily; by contrast, even in the heavy volume days in 1929, trading never went above 16 million shares. Papers stacked on desks. A (now old) joke formed: If a fan blew the wrong way in a Wall Street office, visitors below could expect a ticker-tape parade. “Everybody agreed that the securities-processing system had virtually broken down, and the only major point of dispute was who was more responsible for the mess: the back offices of the brokerage firms of the stock-transfer agents,” Securities and Exchange Commission Commissioner Ray Garrett, Jr. said in 1974. Some 100 broker-dealers failed, crumbling under the pressure of fulfilling those back-orders. The fix: an organization akin to the FDIC, the Securities Investor Protection Corporation. Wall Street would stick to the shortened weeks from June to December; in January, Wednesday trading resumed, though it ended early at 2 for another seven months.

There are few different types of MI you can choose from, they are: Borrower-Paid Monthly (this is what most people think of when they think MI) Borrower-Paid Single Premium (you may have QM issues on this) Lender Paid Single Premium Split Up-front and Monthly The only way to determine which option will ultimately cost you less is to come up with a time estimate or range for how long you anticipate you will hold this mortgage, then look at each option over that time, and see where they fall. To answer your question about the single-premium being added to your loan, this typically does not happen (outside of FHA/VA).  The reason for that is you would now have 90%+ financing and fall into a new pricing bracket, if not being disqualified altogether.  What is far more typical is the use of premium pricing to pay this up-front premium.  Premium pricing is where you take a lender credit in exchange for an elevated rate; it is the exact opposite of paying points to buy down your rate. For example:  say a zero point rate is 4.25%, and you have monthly MI of say .8%.  Your effective rate would be 5.05%.  It may be possible to use premium pricing at an elevated rate of say 4.75% to pay your MI up front--now your effective rate is the note rate of 4.75%.  This is how a single premium can save you money.  Keep in mind though, the 4.75% will be your rate for the life of the loan, and in the other scenario, once the MI drops off, the effective rate will go back down from 5.05% to 4.25%.  This is why it is critical to know your estimated length of financing.

Capital gains tax is a tax on the profit you make when you sell an asset for more than you paid for it. When you sell an asset you have held for a long time, the profit you make is considered a long-term capital gain. Long-term capital gains are taxed at a lower rate than short-term capital gains, which are profits from assets you have held for a shorter period of time.The reason for this is that the government wants to encourage long-term investment in the economy. By taxing long-term capital gains at a lower rate, it becomes more attractive for people to hold onto their assets for a longer period of time, which can help to create a more stable investment environment. This is seen as beneficial for the overall economy because it can help to encourage economic growth and development.Of course, there are limits to this tax preference for long-term investments. In the United States, for example, there are limits on how much of your capital gains can be taxed at the lower long-term rate. In addition, some types of assets, such as collectibles and certain types of real estate, are taxed at a higher rate, regardless of how long they are held.
